Step 1 (Define events for Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion): A number \(x \in S\) has \(7\) digits formed from \(\{ 0,1,2\}\) with first digit \(d_{1} \in \{ 1,2\}\).

The remaining \(5\) positions (including the first digit) can each be filled with \(1\) or \(2\) in \(2^{5}\) ways:
\[|A| = \binom{6}{2} \times 2^{5} = 15 \times 32 = 480\]

• Case 1 (First digit is \(1\)): One more \(1\) is placed in the remaining \(6\) positions in \(\binom{6}{1}\) ways, and the other \(5\) positions are filled from \(\{ 0,2\}\) in \(2^{5}\) ways: \(\binom{6}{1} \times 2^{5} = 6 \times 32 = 192\).
• Case 2 (First digit is \(2\)): Two \(1\)s are placed in the remaining \(6\) positions in \(\binom{6}{2}\) ways, and the other \(4\) positions are filled from \(\{ 0,2\}\) in \(2^{4}\) ways: \(\binom{6}{2} \times 2^{4} = 15 \times 16 = 240\).
\[|B| = 192 + 240 = 432\]
Step 4 (Calculate \(|A \cap B|\)): Both \(0\) and \(1\) appear exactly twice (so \(2\) appears \(3\) times):
• Case 1 (First digit is \(1\)): Choose \(2\) positions for \(0\) and \(1\) position for the second \(1\) from the remaining \(6\) positions: \(\binom{6}{2}\binom{4}{1} = 15 \times 4 = 60\).
• Case 2 (First digit is \(2\)): Choose \(2\) positions for \(0\) and \(2\) positions for \(1\) from the remaining \(6\) positions: \(\binom{6}{2}\binom{4}{2} = 15 \times 6 = 90\).
\[|A \cap B| = 60 + 90 = 150\]

\[|A \cup B| = 480 + 432 - 150 = 762\]
Hence the answer is 762.

For any three points on a parabola, the area \(\Delta_{1}\) of the triangle formed by the three points is exactly twice the area \(\Delta_{2}\) of the triangle formed by the tangents at those three points:
\[\frac{\Delta_{1}}{\Delta_{2}} = 2.\]

\[S = \frac{\alpha}{\beta} + \frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{(\alpha + \beta)^{2} - 2\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta} = \frac{3p^{3}}{p^{3} + q} - 2 = \frac{p^{3} - 2q}{p^{3} + q},\quad P = \frac{\alpha}{\beta} \cdot \frac{\beta}{\alpha} = 1.\]

\(\Rightarrow\) the equation of the line is \(x\cos\alpha + y\sin\alpha = p\)
\(\Rightarrow (\sqrt{3} + 1)x + (\sqrt{3} - 1)y = 8\sqrt{2}\)
or \((\sqrt{3} - 1)x + (\sqrt{3} + 1)y = 8\sqrt{2}\)
Hence options (C) and (D) are both correct.

IIT200204111Q03:
Given that \(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n} > 0\) and \(a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{n - 1}a_{n}=c\).
Apply the Arithmetic Mean--Geometric Mean (AM--GM) Inequality to the \(n\) positive numbers \(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n - 1},2a_{n}\):
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n - 1} + 2a_{n}}{n} \geq \left( a_{1} \cdot a_{2}\cdots a_{n - 1} \cdot (2a_{n}) \right)^{1/n}=(2c)^{1/n} \\ \Longrightarrow a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n - 1} + 2a_{n} \geq n(2c)^{1/n}\end{gathered}\]
Equality holds when \(a_{1}=a_{2}=\cdots=a_{n - 1}=2a_{n}=(2c)^{1/n}\). Thus, the minimum value is \(n(2c)^{1/n}\).
IIT200204111Q04:
Since \(a,b,c\) are in A.P. with common difference \(d > 0\) (as \(a < b < c\)), write \(a=b - d\) and \(c=b + d\). Given \(a + b + c=\frac{3}{2}\):
\[(b - d) + b + (b + d)=\frac{3}{2} \Longrightarrow 3b=\frac{3}{2} \Longrightarrow b=\frac{1}{2}\]
Since \(a^{2},b^{2},c^{2}\) are in G.P., we have \(\left( b^{2} \right)^{2}=a^{2}c^{2} \Longrightarrow b^{2}= \pm ac\).
Substituting \(a=\frac{1}{2} - d\), \(b=\frac{1}{2}\), and \(c=\frac{1}{2} + d\):
\[\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2}= \pm \left( \frac{1}{2} - d \right)\left( \frac{1}{2} + d \right) \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{4}= \pm \left( \frac{1}{4} - d^{2} \right)\]
• If we take the \(+\) sign: \(\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4} - d^{2} \Longrightarrow d=0\), which contradicts \(a < b < c\).
• If we take the \(-\) sign: \(\frac{1}{4}=d^{2} - \frac{1}{4} \Longrightarrow d^{2}=\frac{1}{2} \Longrightarrow d=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) (since \(d > 0\)).
Therefore:
\[a=b - d=\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]

The word BANANA consists of \(6\) letters: \(3\) A's, \(2\) N's, and \(1\) B.
1. Total permutations of BANANA without restriction:
\[N_{\text{total}}=\frac{6!}{3!\ 2!}=\frac{720}{6 \times 2}=60\]
2. Permutations in which the two N's are together:
Treat (NN) as a single unit along with A, A, A, B (\(5\) objects in total, of which \(3\) are identical A's):
\[N_{\text{together}}=\frac{5!}{3!}=\frac{120}{6}=20\]
Subtracting the two gives the number of arrangements where the two N's are not adjacent:
\[N_{\text{non}-\text{adjacent}}=60 - 20=40\]

\[\sum_{i=0}^{m}\ \binom{10}{i}\binom{20}{m - i}=\binom{30}{m}\]

IIT200204111Q07:
For a system of two linear equations \(a_{1}x + b_{1}y=c_{1}\) and \(a_{2}x + b_{2}y=c_{2}\) to have infinitely many solutions, the ratios of coefficients must be equal:
\[\frac{k + 1}{k}=\frac{8}{k + 3}=\frac{4k}{3k - 1}\]
Equating the first two ratios:
\[(k + 1)(k + 3)=8k \Longrightarrow k^{2} + 4k + 3=8k \Longrightarrow k^{2} - 4k + 3=0 \Longrightarrow (k - 1)(k - 3)=0\]
So \(k=1\) or \(k=3\). Now test both in the third ratio \(\frac{4k}{3k - 1}\):
• For \(k=1\): \(\frac{k + 1}{k}=2\), \(\frac{8}{k + 3}=2\), and \(\frac{4(1)}{3(1) - 1}=\frac{4}{2}=2\) (All three ratios equal \(2\)).
• For \(k=3\): \(\frac{k + 1}{k}=\frac{4}{3}\), \(\frac{8}{k + 3}=\frac{4}{3}\), whereas \(\frac{4(3)}{3(3) - 1}=\frac{12}{8}=\frac{3}{2} \neq \frac{4}{3}\) (No solution for \(k=3\)).
Hence, there is exactly \(1\) value of \(k\) (\(k=1\)).
IIT200204111Q08:
Split the inequality into two cases based on the sign of \((x + 2)\):
1. Case 1 (\(x \geq - 2\)): Here \(|x + 2|=x + 2\). The inequality becomes:
\[x^{2} - (x + 2) + x > 0 \Longrightarrow x^{2} - 2 > 0 \Longrightarrow \left(x - \sqrt{2}\right)\left(x + \sqrt{2}\right) > 0\]
Intersecting with \(x \geq - 2\) gives:
\[x \in [ - 2, - \sqrt{2}) \cup \left(\sqrt{2},\infty\right)\]
2. Case 2 (\(x < - 2\)): Here \(|x + 2|= - (x + 2)\). The inequality becomes:
\[x^{2} + (x + 2) + x > 0 \Longrightarrow x^{2} + 2x + 2 > 0 \Longrightarrow (x + 1)^{2} + 1 > 0\]
which holds true for all real \(x\). Intersecting with \(x < - 2\) gives:
\[x \in ( - \infty, - 2)\]
Taking the union of both cases:
\[x \in ( - \infty, - 2) \cup [ - 2, - \sqrt{2}) \cup \left(\sqrt{2},\infty\right)=\left( - \infty, - \sqrt{2}\right) \cup \left(\sqrt{2},\infty\right)\]

\[f(x)=3\sin x - 4\sin^{3}x=\sin 3x\]

For \(n=0\), the interval of increase is \(\left[ - \frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6} \right]\), whose length is:

IIT200204111Q10:
In any acute-angled \(\triangle ABC\), by the Sine Rule:
\[\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}=2R\]
• In (A), knowing \(a,\sin A,\sin B\) uniquely determines \(A,B\) (since the triangle is acute-angled), hence \(C=\pi - (A + B)\), and all three sides \(a,b,c\).
• In (B), knowing all three sides \(a,b,c\) uniquely determines the triangle by SSS congruence.
• In (C), knowing \(a,\sin B,R\) gives \(\sin A=\frac{a}{2R}\), so acute angles \(A\) and \(B\) (and thus \(C,b,c\)) are uniquely determined.
• In (D), the relation \(a=2R\sin A\) makes \(a,\sin A,R\) dependent (\(R=\frac{a}{2\sin A}\) provides no new independent information beyond \(a\) and \(A\)).
Infinitely many acute-angled triangles can have a given side \(a\) and opposite angle \(A\).
Thus, (D) does not uniquely determine the triangle.
IIT200204111Q11:
The range of \(a\cos x + b\sin x\) is \(\left[ - \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}},\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}} \right]\). For \(7\cos x + 5\sin x=2k + 1\) to have a real solution:
\[- \sqrt{7^{2} + 5^{2}} \leq 2k + 1 \leq \sqrt{7^{2} + 5^{2}} \Longrightarrow - \sqrt{74} \leq 2k + 1 \leq \sqrt{74}\]
Since \(\sqrt{74} \approx 8.602\):
\[- 8.602 \leq 2k + 1 \leq 8.602 \Longrightarrow - 9.602 \leq 2k \leq 7.602 \Longrightarrow - 4.801 \leq k \leq 3.801\]
The integral values of \(k\) in this interval are \(k \in \{ - 4, - 3, - 2, - 1,0,1,2,3\}\), which gives \(8\) integral values.

Rewrite the two parallel lines in identical normal/coefficient form:
\[L_{1}:4x + 2y - 9=0\quad \text{ and }\quad L_{2}:4x + 2y + 12=0\]
Notice that the origin \(O(0,0)\) lies between the two parallel lines because \(- 9 < 0\) and \(+ 12 > 0\) have opposite signs.

Hence, \(O\) divides the segment \(PQ\) in the ratio \(3:4\).

For any real \(m\), the line \(mx - y - b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}=0\) is already tangent to the first circle \(x^{2} + y^{2}=b^{2}\) (since its perpendicular distance from \((0,0)\) is \(\frac{b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}{\sqrt{m^{2} + 1}}=b\)).
For this line to also be tangent to the second circle \((x - a)^{2} + y^{2}=b^{2}\), its perpendicular distance from the centre \(C_{2}(a,0)\) must equal the radius \(b\):
\[\frac{\left| ma - 0 - b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}} \right|}{\sqrt{m^{2} + 1}}=b \Longrightarrow \left| ma - b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}} \right|=b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\]
Since \(m > 0\) and \(a > 2b > 0\), taking the non-zero case gives:
\[ma - b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}=b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}} \Longrightarrow ma=2b\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\]
Squaring both sides:
\[m^{2}a^{2}=4b^{2}(1 + m^{2}) \Longrightarrow m^{2}(a^{2} - 4b^{2})=4b^{2} \Longrightarrow m=\frac{2b}{\sqrt{a^{2} - 4b^{2}}}\]

The focus of the parabola \(y^{2}=4ax\) is \(S(a,0)\), and any moving point on it can be parameterized as \(P(at^{2},2at)\). Let \(M(h,k)\) be the midpoint of \(SP\):
\[h=\frac{a + at^{2}}{2} \Longrightarrow at^{2}=2h - a,\quad k=\frac{0 + 2at}{2}=at \Longrightarrow t=\frac{k}{a}\]
Eliminating the parameter \(t\):
\[a\left( \frac{k}{a} \right)^{2}=2h - a \Longrightarrow k^{2}=2a\left( h - \frac{a}{2} \right)\]
Replacing \((h,k)\) by \((x,y)\), the locus is the parabola:
\[y^{2}=4\left( \frac{a}{2} \right)\left( x - \frac{a}{2} \right)\]
Here \(X=x - \frac{a}{2}\) and focal length \(A=\frac{a}{2}\). Its directrix is given by:
\[X= - A \Longrightarrow x - \frac{a}{2}= - \frac{a}{2} \Longrightarrow x=0\]

Each side of this square has length \(s=\sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}}=\sqrt{2}\), so the enclosed area is:
\[\text{Area}=s^{2}=\left( \sqrt{2} \right)^{2}=2\text{ sq. units}\]
(Equivalently, \(\text{Area}=\int_{- 1}^{1}\ \left[ (1 - |x|) - (|x| - 1) \right] dx=4\int_{0}^{1}\ (1 - x) dx=2\).)

Interchanging \(x\) and \(y\) gives:

Differentiating \(f(x)=2x + \sin x\) with respect to \(x\):
\[f'(x)=2 + \cos x\]
Since \(- 1 \leq \cos x \leq 1\) for all \(x\mathbb{\in \mathbb{R}}\), we have:
\[f'(x)=2 + \cos x \geq 2 - 1=1 > 0\quad \forall x\mathbb{\in \mathbb{R}}\]
Thus, \(f(x)\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\) and is one-to-one (injective). Furthermore, since \(f(x)\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\) and:
\[\lim\limits_{x \to - \infty}(2x + \sin x)= - \infty,\quad \lim\limits_{x \to + \infty}(2x + \sin x)= + \infty\]
by the Intermediate Value Theorem, the range of \(f\) is \(( - \infty,\infty)=\mathbb{R}\), so \(f\) is onto (surjective).
IIT200204111Q21:
Rewrite \(f(x)\) explicitly on the three intervals:
\[f(x)=\left\{ \begin{matrix} \frac{1}{2}( - x - 1), & x < - 1 \\ \tan^{- 1}x, & - 1 \leq x \leq 1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x - 1), & x > 1 \end{matrix} \right.\]
Check continuity at the transition points \(x=1\) and \(x= - 1\):
• At \(x=1\): \(\lim\limits_{x \to 1^{-}}f(x)=\tan^{- 1}(1)=\frac{\pi}{4}\), whereas \(\lim\limits_{x \to 1^{+}}f(x)=\frac{1}{2}(1 - 1)=0\).
Since \(\frac{\pi}{4} \neq 0\), \(f(x)\) is discontinuous (and hence non-differentiable) at \(x=1\).
• At \(x= - 1\): \(\lim\limits_{x \to - 1^{+}}f(x)=\tan^{- 1}( - 1)= - \frac{\pi}{4}\), whereas \(\lim\limits_{x \to - 1^{-}}f(x)=\frac{1}{2}(1 - 1)=0\).
Since \(- \frac{\pi}{4} \neq 0\), \(f(x)\) is discontinuous (and hence non-differentiable) at \(x= - 1\).
At every other real number \(x\mathbb{\in \mathbb{R} -}\{ - 1,1\}\), \(f(x)\) is clearly differentiable. Thus, the domain of \(f'(x)\) is \(\mathbb{R -}\{ - 1,1\}\).
IIT200204111Q22:
Using Maclaurin series expansions as \(x \to 0\):
\[\begin{gathered}\cos x - 1= - \frac{x^{2}}{2!} + \frac{x^{4}}{4!} - \cdots= - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + O(x^{4}) \\ \cos x - e^{x}=\left( 1 - \frac{x^{2}}{2!} + \cdots \right) - \left( 1 + x + \frac{x^{2}}{2!} + \cdots \right)= - x - x^{2} + O(x^{3})\end{gathered}\]
Multiplying the two factors together:
\[(\cos x - 1)(\cos x - e^{x})=\left( - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + O(x^{4}) \right)\left( - x - x^{2} + O(x^{3}) \right)=\frac{1}{2}x^{3} + \frac{1}{2}x^{4} + O(x^{5})\]
For \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{(\cos x - 1)(\cos x - e^{x})}{x^{n}}\) to be a finite non-zero number (namely \(\frac{1}{2}\)), we must have \(n=3\).
IIT200204111Q23:
As \(x \to 0\), \(\frac{f(1 + x)}{f(1)} \to \frac{f(1)}{f(1)}=1\) (since \(f\) is differentiable at \(x=1\) and hence continuous), so the limit is of the indeterminate form \(1^{\infty}\):
\[L=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left( 1 + \frac{f(1 + x) - f(1)}{f(1)} \right)^{1/x}=\exp \left( \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{f(1 + x) - f(1)}{f(1)} \right)\]
By the definition of the derivative \(f'(1)=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{f(1 + x) - f(1)}{x}\):
\[L=\exp \left( \frac{f'(1)}{f(1)} \right)=e^{6/3}=e^{2}\]

IIT200204111Q24.t:
{{figure}}
Differentiating the implicit curve \(y^{3} + 3x^{2}=12y\) with respect to \(x\):
\[3y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} + 6x=12\frac{dy}{dx} \Longrightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{6x}{12 - 3y^{2}}=\frac{2x}{4 - y^{2}}\]
The tangent is vertical where \(\frac{dx}{dy}=0\) (and \(x \neq 0\)), which gives:
\[4 - y^{2}=0 \Longrightarrow y= \pm 2\]
Substitute \(y= \pm 2\) into the curve equation \(3x^{2}=12y - y^{3}\):
• For \(y= - 2\): \(3x^{2}=12( - 2) - ( - 2)^{3}= - 24 + 8= - 16 < 0\) (no real solution for \(x\)).
• For \(y=2\): \(3x^{2}=12(2) - 2^{3}=24 - 8=16 \Longrightarrow x^{2}=\frac{16}{3} \Longrightarrow x= \pm \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}\).
Hence, the points with vertical tangents are \(\left( \pm \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}},2 \right)\).

IIT200204111Q25.t:
{{figure}}
For the parabola \(y^{2}=8x=4(2)x\), we have \(a=2\). Any tangent of slope \(m\) to \(y^{2}=8x\) has the equation:
\[y=mx + \frac{2}{m}\]
Substitute this line into the rectangular hyperbola \(xy= - 1\):
\[x\left( mx + \frac{2}{m} \right)= - 1 \Longrightarrow m^{2}x^{2} + 2x + m=0\]
For the line to be tangent to \(xy= - 1\), the discriminant of this quadratic in \(x\) must be zero (\(D=0\)):
\[D=2^{2} - 4(m^{2})(m)=4 - 4m^{3}=0 \Longrightarrow m^{3}=1 \Longrightarrow m=1\]
Substituting \(m=1\) into \(y=mx + \frac{2}{m}\) gives the common tangent:
\[y=x + 2\]

IIT200204111Q26:
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Newton--Leibniz Rule), for \(x \in \left[ - \sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}\right]\):
\[f'(x)=\sqrt{2 - x^{2}}\]
The equation \(x^{2} - f'(x)=0\) becomes:
\[x^{2}=\sqrt{2 - x^{2}}\quad (x^{2} \leq 2)\]
Squaring both sides:
\[x^{4}=2 - x^{2} \Longrightarrow x^{4} + x^{2} - 2=0 \Longrightarrow (x^{2} - 1)(x^{2} + 2)=0\]
Since \(x\) is real, \(x^{2} + 2 \neq 0\), so \(x^{2}=1 \Longrightarrow x= \pm 1\).
IIT200204111Q27:
Substitute \(u=2x\) so that \(du=2\ dx \Longrightarrow dx=\frac{1}{2}\ du\). When \(x=3\), \(u=6\); when \(x=3 + 3T\), \(u=6 + 6T\):
\[J=\int_{3}^{3 + 3T}\ f(2x) dx=\frac{1}{2}\int_{6}^{6 + 6T}\ f(u) du\]
Since \(f(u)\) is periodic with period \(T\), its integral over any interval of length \(6T\) equals \(6\) times its integral over one period \([0,T]\):
\[J=\frac{1}{2} \times 6\int_{0}^{T}\ f(u) du=3I\]
IIT200204111Q28:
Split the integral into two parts:
\[I=\int_{- 1/2}^{1/2}\ [x] dx + \int_{- 1/2}^{1/2}\ \ln \left( \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} \right)dx=I_{1} + I_{2}\]
1. Evaluate \(I_{2}\): Since \(h(x)=\ln \left( \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} \right)\) satisfies \(h( - x)=\ln \left( \frac{1 - x}{1 + x} \right)= - h(x)\), \(h(x)\) is an odd function on \(\left[ - \frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2} \right]\), so \(I_{2}=0\).
2. Evaluate \(I_{1}\): On \(\left[ - \frac{1}{2},0 \right)\), \([x]= - 1\), and on \(\left[ 0,\frac{1}{2} \right)\), \([x]=0\):
\[I_{1}=\int_{- 1/2}^{0}\ ( - 1) dx + \int_{0}^{1/2}\ 0\ dx= - \frac{1}{2} + 0= - \frac{1}{2}\]
Therefore, \(I= - \frac{1}{2}\).
IIT200204111Q29:
Given \(\left| \overrightarrow{a} \right|=1\), \(\left| \overrightarrow{b} \right|=1\), and \(\left(\overrightarrow{a} + 2\overrightarrow{b}\right)\bot\left(5\overrightarrow{a} - 4\overrightarrow{b}\right)\), their dot product vanishes:
\[\begin{gathered}\left(\overrightarrow{a} + 2\overrightarrow{b}\right) \cdot \left(5\overrightarrow{a} - 4\overrightarrow{b}\right)=0 \\ 5\left| \overrightarrow{a} \right|^{2} - 4\left(\overrightarrow{a} \cdot \overrightarrow{b}\right) + 10\left(\overrightarrow{a} \cdot \overrightarrow{b}\right) - 8\left| \overrightarrow{b} \right|^{2}=0 \Longrightarrow 5(1) + 6\left(\overrightarrow{a} \cdot \overrightarrow{b}\right) - 8(1)=0 \\ 6\left| \overrightarrow{a} \right|\left| \overrightarrow{b} \right|\cos \theta=3 \Longrightarrow \cos \theta=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2} \Longrightarrow \theta=60^{\circ}\end{gathered}\]
IIT200204111Q30:
By definition of the scalar triple product:
\[\left[ \overrightarrow{U}\quad \overrightarrow{V}\quad \overrightarrow{W} \right]=\overrightarrow{U} \cdot \left( \overrightarrow{V} \times \overrightarrow{W} \right)=\left| \overrightarrow{U} \right|\ \left| \overrightarrow{V} \times \overrightarrow{W} \right|\cos \theta\]
First compute the cross product \(\overrightarrow{V} \times \overrightarrow{W}\):
\[\overrightarrow{V} \times \overrightarrow{W}=\left| \begin{matrix} \widehat{i} & \widehat{j} & \widehat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{matrix} \right|=\widehat{i}(3 - 0) - \widehat{j}(6 - ( - 1)) + \widehat{k}(0 - 1)=3\widehat{i} - 7\widehat{j} - \widehat{k}\]
Since \(\left| \overrightarrow{U} \right|=1\) and \(\text{maxcos}\theta=1\) (when \(\overrightarrow{U}\) is parallel to \(\overrightarrow{V} \times \overrightarrow{W}\)):
\[\max \left[ \overrightarrow{U}\quad \overrightarrow{V}\quad \overrightarrow{W} \right]=\left| \overrightarrow{V} \times \overrightarrow{W} \right|=\sqrt{3^{2} + ( - 7)^{2} + ( - 1)^{2}}=\sqrt{9 + 49 + 1}=\sqrt{59}\]
IIT200304201Q01:
Given the function \(f:[0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)\) defined by:
\[f(x)=\frac{x}{1 + x}=1 - \frac{1}{1 + x}\]
Step 1: Check for Injectivity (One-One):
Differentiating \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\) on \((0,\infty)\):
\[f\prime(x)=\frac{(1 + x)(1) - x(1)}{(1 + x)^{2}}=\frac{1}{(1 + x)^{2}} > 0\quad \forall x \in [0,\infty)\]
Since \(f\prime(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in [0,\infty)\), the function \(f(x)\) is strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\) and is therefore one-one (injective).
Step 2: Check for Surjectivity (Onto):
At \(x=0\), we have \(f(0)=0\). Taking the limit as \(x \to \infty\):
\[\lim\limits_{x \to \infty}f(x)=\lim\limits_{x \to \infty}\frac{1}{\frac{1}{x} + 1}=1\]
Since \(f(x)\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\), the range of \(f\) is:
\[\text{Range}(f)=[0,1) \neq [0,\infty)(\text{Codomain})\]
Because the range is a proper subset of the codomain \([0,\infty)\), \(f\) is not onto (not surjective). Hence, \(f\) is one-one but not onto.

IIT200304201Q03.t:
{{figure}}
For Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT) to be applicable to \(f(x)\) on \([0,1]\), \(f(x)\) must be continuous on \([0,1]\) and differentiable on \((0,1)\).
Let us examine option (a) at the interior point \(x=\frac{1}{2} \in (0,1)\):
• Left-Hand Derivative (LHD) at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\):
\[\text{LHD}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{f\left( \frac{1}{2} + h \right) - f\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{\left( \frac{1}{2} - \left( \frac{1}{2} + h \right) \right) - 0}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{- h}{h}= - 1\]
• Right-Hand Derivative (RHD) at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\):
\[\text{RHD}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f\left( \frac{1}{2} + h \right) - f\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{\left( \frac{1}{2} - \left( \frac{1}{2} + h \right) \right)^{2} - 0}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{h^{2}}{h}=0\]
Since \(\text{LHD} \neq \text{RHD}\) at \(x=\frac{1}{2}\), \(f(x)\) in (a) is not differentiable at \(x=\frac{1}{2} \in (0,1)\). Meanwhile, on \([0,1]\):
• In (b), \(f(x)\) is analytic everywhere (since \(\frac{\sin x}{x}=1 - \frac{x^{2}}{3!} + \frac{x^{4}}{5!} - \cdots\)).
• In (c), for \(x \in [0,1]\), \(f(x)=x|x|=x^{2}\), which is a polynomial.
• In (d), for \(x \in [0,1]\), \(f(x)=|x|=x\), which is continuous on \([0,1]\) and differentiable on \((0,1)\).
Thus, LMVT is not applicable to (a).

IIT200304201Q04.t:
{{figure}}
For the given ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{9} + \frac{y^{2}}{5}=1\), we have \(a^{2}=9 \Longrightarrow a=3\) and \(b^{2}=5 \Longrightarrow b=\sqrt{5}\).
Step 1: Find the eccentricity and coordinates of the ends of the latus rectum:
\[e=\sqrt{1 - \frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}}=\sqrt{1 - \frac{5}{9}}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}}=\frac{2}{3}\]
Hence, \(ae=3 \times \frac{2}{3}=2\) and \(\frac{b^{2}}{a}=\frac{5}{3}\). The four endpoints of the latus recta are \(\left( \pm 2, \pm \frac{5}{3} \right)\).
Step 2: Equation of the tangent in the first quadrant:
The equation of the tangent to \(\frac{x^{2}}{9} + \frac{y^{2}}{5}=1\) at \(L\left( 2,\frac{5}{3} \right)\) is:
\[\frac{x(2)}{9} + \frac{y\left( \frac{5}{3} \right)}{5}=1 \Longrightarrow \frac{2x}{9} + \frac{y}{3}=1\]
This tangent meets the coordinate axes at \(A\left( \frac{9}{2},0 \right)\) and \(B(0,3)\).
Step 3: Compute the area of the rhombus \(ABCD\):
By symmetry of the ellipse about both coordinate axes, the four tangents form a rhombus \(ABCD\) whose area is \(4\) times the area of the right-angled triangle \(\triangle OAB\) in the first quadrant:
\[\text{Area}=4 \times \left( \frac{1}{2} \times OA \times OB \right)=2 \times \frac{9}{2} \times 3=27\text{ sq. units}\]

IIT200304201Q05.t:
{{figure}}
The triangle is bounded by the lines \(x=0\), \(y=0\), and \(x + y=21\).
For a point \((x,y)\) with \(x,y \in {\mathbb{Z}}\) to lie strictly inside the triangle, it must satisfy:
\[x > 0,\quad y > 0,\quad \text{ and }\quad x + y < 21 \Longrightarrow x \geq 1,\quad y \geq 1,\quad x + y \leq 20\]
For each integer value of \(x \in \{1,2,3,\ldots,19\}\), the integer coordinate \(y\) can take values from \(1\) up to \(20 - x\), giving \((20 - x)\) integral points.
Summing over all valid values of \(x\):
\[\text{Total Interior Integral Points}=\sum_{x=1}^{19}\ (20 - x)=19 + 18 + 17 + \cdots + 1=\frac{19 \times 20}{2}=190\]

IIT200304201Q06:
Computing the matrix product \(A^{2}=A \cdot A\):
\[A^{2}=\begin{bmatrix} \alpha & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \alpha & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} \alpha^{2} & 0 \\ \alpha + 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]
Equating \(A^{2}=B\):
\[\begin{bmatrix} \alpha^{2} & 0 \\ \alpha + 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]
Comparing the corresponding matrix entries gives the simultaneous conditions:
1. \(\alpha^{2}=1 \Longrightarrow \alpha=1\text{ or }\alpha= - 1\)
2. \(\alpha + 1=5 \Longrightarrow \alpha=4\)
Since both conditions cannot be satisfied simultaneously, there is no real value of \(\alpha\) for which \(A^{2}=B\).
IIT200304201Q07:
The given line passes through the point \(P(4,2,k)\) and has direction ratios \(\overrightarrow{b}=(1,1,2)\).
The normal vector to the plane \(2x - 4y + z=7\) is \(\overrightarrow{n}=(2, - 4,1)\).
Step 1: Verify that the line is parallel to the plane:
\[\overrightarrow{b} \cdot \overrightarrow{n}=(1)(2) + (1)( - 4) + (2)(1)=2 - 4 + 2=0\]
Since \(\overrightarrow{b} \cdot \overrightarrow{n}=0\), the line is perpendicular to the normal of the plane.
Step 2: Require the point \(P(4,2,k)\) on the line to lie in the plane:
\[2(4) - 4(2) + k=7 \Longrightarrow 8 - 8 + k=7 \Longrightarrow k=7\]

IIT200304201Q08.t:
{{figure}}
Let the angles of \(\triangle ABC\) be \(4\theta\), \(\theta\), and \(\theta\). Since the sum of angles in a triangle is \(180^{\circ}\):
\[4\theta + \theta + \theta=180^{\circ} \Longrightarrow 6\theta=180^{\circ} \Longrightarrow \theta=30^{\circ}\]
Thus, the angles are \(A=120^{\circ}\), \(B=30^{\circ}\), and \(C=30^{\circ}\). By the Sine Rule:
\[\frac{a}{\sin 120^{\circ}}=\frac{b}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=\frac{c}{\sin 30^{\circ}} \Longrightarrow a:b:c=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}:\frac{1}{2}:\frac{1}{2}=\sqrt{3}:1:1\]
The longest side is \(a=\sqrt{3}k\), and the perimeter is \(a + b + c=\left(\sqrt{3} + 1 + 1\right)k=\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)k\). Therefore, the required ratio is:
\[\frac{\text{Longest Side}}{\text{Perimeter}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2 + \sqrt{3}}\quad \text{ or }\quad \sqrt{3}:\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)\]

IIT200304201Q09:
Rewrite the given limit by grouping standard trigonometric limits as \(x \to 0\):
\[\begin{gathered}L=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left( \frac{\sin nx}{nx} \cdot n \cdot \frac{(a - n)nx - \tan x}{x} \right) \\ L=n\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left( \frac{\sin nx}{nx} \right) \cdot \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\left( (a - n)n - \frac{\tan x}{x} \right)\end{gathered}\]
Since \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin nx}{nx}=1\) and \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\tan x}{x}=1\), we obtain:
\[L=n \cdot 1 \cdot \left( (a - n)n - 1 \right)=0\]
Since \(n \neq 0\), we have:
\[(a - n)n - 1=0 \Longrightarrow a - n=\frac{1}{n} \Longrightarrow a=n + \frac{1}{n}\]
IIT200304201Q10:
The total number of ways to select \(2\) numbers from \(S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) without replacement is:
\[n(\Omega)=\binom{6}{2}=\frac{6 \times 5}{2}=15\]
Let \(E\) be the event that the minimum of the two chosen numbers is strictly less than \(4\).
The complementary event \(\overline{E}\) is that both selected numbers are greater than or equal to \(4\), which means both numbers are chosen from the subset \(\{4,5,6\}\):
\[n\left(\overline{E}\right)=\binom{3}{2}=3\]
Therefore, the required probability is:
\[P(E)=1 - P\left(\overline{E}\right)=1 - \frac{3}{15}=1 - \frac{1}{5}=\frac{4}{5}\]

IIT200304201Q11.t:
{{figure}}
Comparing the given hyperbola \(\frac{x^{2}}{\cos^{2}\alpha} - \frac{y^{2}}{\sin^{2}\alpha}=1\) with the standard form \(\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1\), we have:
\[a^{2}=\cos^{2}\alpha\quad \text{ and }\quad b^{2}=\sin^{2}\alpha\]
Using the fundamental relation \(b^{2}=a^{2}(e^{2} - 1)\), we compute the distance from the centre to the foci (\(ae\)):
\[a^{2}e^{2}=a^{2} + b^{2}=\cos^{2}\alpha + \sin^{2}\alpha=1 \Longrightarrow ae=1\]
Thus, the coordinates of the foci are \(( \pm ae,0)=( \pm 1,0)\), which are completely independent of \(\alpha\). Meanwhile:
• Abscissae of vertices \(= \pm a= \pm \left| \cos \alpha \right|\) (varies with \(\alpha\)).
• Eccentricity \(e=\frac{1}{\left| \cos \alpha \right|}=\left| \sec \alpha \right|\) (varies with \(\alpha\)).
• Directrices \(x= \pm \frac{a}{e}= \pm \cos^{2}\alpha\) (varies with \(\alpha\)).
Hence, the abscissae of foci remain constant.

IIT200304201Q12:
Rewrite \(f(x)\) by completing the square in the denominator:
\[f(x)=\frac{(x^{2} + x + 1) + 1}{x^{2} + x + 1}=1 + \frac{1}{x^{2} + x + 1}=1 + \frac{1}{\left( x + \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4}}\]
Since \(\left( x + \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} \geq 0\) for all \(x \in {\mathbb{R}}\), the denominator \(D(x)=\left( x + \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4}\) satisfies:
\[\frac{3}{4} \leq \left( x + \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4} < \infty\]
Taking the reciprocal and adding \(1\):
\[0 < \frac{1}{\left( x + \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4}} \leq \frac{4}{3} \Longrightarrow 1 < 1 + \frac{1}{x^{2} + x + 1} \leq 1 + \frac{4}{3}=\frac{7}{3}\]
Therefore, the range of \(f(x)\) is \(\left( 1,\frac{7}{3} \right]\).
IIT200304201Q13:
Since \(f\) is differentiable at \(x=2\) and \(x=1\), we can use the definition of the derivative (or L'Hôpital's Rule with respect to \(h\)):
\[L=\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\left[ \frac{f(2 + 2h + h^{2}) - f(2)}{2h + h^{2}} \cdot \frac{h - h^{2}}{f(1 + h - h^{2}) - f(1)} \cdot \frac{2h + h^{2}}{h - h^{2}} \right]\]
As \(h \to 0\), both \(\Delta_{1}=2h + h^{2} \to 0\) and \(\Delta_{2}=h - h^{2} \to 0\). Therefore:
\[L=\frac{f\prime(2)}{f\prime(1)} \cdot \lim\limits_{h \to 0}\frac{h(2 + h)}{h(1 - h)}=\frac{f\prime(2)}{f\prime(1)} \cdot \frac{2}{1}\]
Substituting \(f\prime(2)=6\) and \(f\prime(1)=4\):
\[L=\frac{6}{4} \times 2=3\]
IIT200304201Q14:
Complete the square for both quadratic functions \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\):
1. For \(f(x)=x^{2} + 2bx + 2c^{2}=(x + b)^{2} + (2c^{2} - b^{2})\):
Since \((x + b)^{2} \geq 0\) for all \(x \in {\mathbb{R}}\), the minimum value is:
\[\min_{x \in {\mathbb{R}}}f(x)=2c^{2} - b^{2}\]
2. For \(g(x)= - x^{2} - 2cx + b^{2}= - (x + c)^{2} + (b^{2} + c^{2})\):
Since \(- (x + c)^{2} \leq 0\) for all \(x \in {\mathbb{R}}\), the maximum value is:
\[\max_{x \in {\mathbb{R}}}g(x)=b^{2} + c^{2}\]
Applying the given condition \(\min f(x) > \max g(x)\):
\[2c^{2} - b^{2} > b^{2} + c^{2} \Longrightarrow c^{2} > 2b^{2} \Longrightarrow |c| > |b|\sqrt{2}\]

IIT200304201Q15.t:
{{figure}}
Factoring the two given quadratic equations into pairs of parallel lines:
\[\begin{gathered}x^{2} - 8x + 12=0 \Longrightarrow (x - 2)(x - 6)=0 \Longrightarrow x=2\text{ and }x=6 \\ y^{2} - 14y + 45=0 \Longrightarrow (y - 5)(y - 9)=0 \Longrightarrow y=5\text{ and }y=9\end{gathered}\]
These four lines form a square of side length \(4\) with vertices \((2,5)\), \((6,5)\), \((6,9)\), and \((2,9)\).
The centre of the inscribed circle coincides with the geometric centre (midpoint of the diagonals) of the square:
\[\text{Centre }C=\left( \frac{2 + 6}{2},\frac{5 + 9}{2} \right)=(4,7)\]

IIT200304201Q16.t:
{{figure}}
For the parabola \(y^{2}=16x=4(4)x\), we have \(a=4\), so its focus is \(S(4,0)\).
Let the slope of the focal chord passing through \(S(4,0)\) be \(m\). Its equation is:
\[y - 0=m(x - 4) \Longrightarrow mx - y - 4m=0\]
The given circle \((x - 6)^{2} + y^{2}=2\) has centre \(C(6,0)\) and radius \(r=\sqrt{2}\).
Since the focal chord is tangent to this circle, the perpendicular distance from \(C(6,0)\) to the line \(mx - y - 4m=0\) equals the radius \(\sqrt{2}\):
\[\frac{\left| m(6) - 0 - 4m \right|}{\sqrt{m^{2} + 1}}=\sqrt{2} \Longrightarrow \frac{|2m|}{\sqrt{m^{2} + 1}}=\sqrt{2}\]
Squaring both sides:
\[4m^{2}=2(m^{2} + 1) \Longrightarrow 2m^{2}=2 \Longrightarrow m^{2}=1 \Longrightarrow m= \pm 1\]
Hence, the possible values of the slope are \(\{ - 1,1\}\).

IIT200304201Q17:
For \(f(x)=\sqrt{\sin^{- 1}(2x) + \frac{\pi}{6}}\) to be defined and real-valued, two conditions must hold simultaneously:
1. Domain of \(\sin^{- 1}(2x)\):
\[- 1 \leq 2x \leq 1\quad \text{ and }\quad - \frac{\pi}{2} \leq \sin^{- 1}(2x) \leq \frac{\pi}{2}\]
2. Non-negativity under the square root:
\[\sin^{- 1}(2x) + \frac{\pi}{6} \geq 0 \Longrightarrow \sin^{- 1}(2x) \geq - \frac{\pi}{6}\]
Combining with the principal value range of \(\sin^{- 1}(2x)\):
\[- \frac{\pi}{6} \leq \sin^{- 1}(2x) \leq \frac{\pi}{2}\]
Since \(\sin \theta\) is strictly increasing on \(\left[ - \frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{2} \right]\):
\[\sin \left( - \frac{\pi}{6} \right) \leq 2x \leq \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \Longrightarrow - \frac{1}{2} \leq 2x \leq 1 \Longrightarrow - \frac{1}{4} \leq x \leq \frac{1}{2}\]
Thus, the domain of \(f(x)\) is \(\left[ - \frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2} \right]\).
IIT200304201Q18:
Given \(|z|=1 \Longrightarrow z\overline{z}=1\). Consider \(\omega + \overline{\omega}\):
\[\omega + \overline{\omega}=\frac{z - 1}{z + 1} + \frac{\overline{z} - 1}{\overline{z} + 1}=\frac{(z - 1)\left(\overline{z} + 1\right) + \left(\overline{z} - 1\right)(z + 1)}{|z + 1|^{2}}\]
Expanding the numerator:
\[\left(z\overline{z} + z - \overline{z} - 1\right) + \left(z\overline{z} + \overline{z} - z - 1\right)=2\left(z\overline{z} - 1\right)\]
Since \(z\overline{z}=|z|^{2}=1\), we get:
\[2\Re(\omega)=\omega + \overline{\omega}=\frac{2(1 - 1)}{|z + 1|^{2}}=0 \Longrightarrow \Re(\omega)=0\]
(Geometric Interpretation: Since \(|z|=1\), \(z\) lies on the unit circle with diameter endpoints \(1\) and \(- 1\).
By Thales' theorem, the vectors \(z - 1\) and \(z + 1\) are perpendicular, so \(\omega=\frac{z - 1}{z + 1}\) is purely imaginary.)
IIT200304201Q19:
For the expression to be real and well-defined, \(\sqrt{x^{2} + x} > 0\). Also, since \(\alpha \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right)\), we have \(\tan \alpha > 0\).
Applying the Arithmetic Mean--Geometric Mean (AM--GM) Inequality to the two positive quantities \(A=\sqrt{x^{2} + x}\) and \(B=\frac{\tan^{2}\alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + x}}\):
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{\sqrt{x^{2} + x} + \frac{\tan^{2}\alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + x}}}{2} \geq \sqrt{\sqrt{x^{2} + x} \cdot \frac{\tan^{2}\alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + x}}}=\sqrt{\tan^{2}\alpha}=\tan \alpha \\ \Longrightarrow \sqrt{x^{2} + x} + \frac{\tan^{2}\alpha}{\sqrt{x^{2} + x}} \geq 2\tan \alpha\end{gathered}\]
Equality holds when \(\sqrt{x^{2} + x}=\tan \alpha\). Thus, the expression is always greater than or equal to \(2\tan \alpha\).
IIT200304201Q20:
Apply integration by parts to \(I(m,n)=\int_{0}^{1}\ (1 + t)^{n} \cdot t^{m}\ dt\), taking the first function as \(u=(1 + t)^{n}\) and the second function as \(dv=t^{m}\ dt\):
\[\begin{gathered}du=n(1 + t)^{n - 1}\ dt,\quad v=\frac{t^{m + 1}}{m + 1} \\ I(m,n)=\left[ \frac{t^{m + 1}(1 + t)^{n}}{m + 1} \right]_{0}^{1} - \int_{0}^{1}\ \frac{t^{m + 1}}{m + 1} \cdot n(1 + t)^{n - 1}\ dt\end{gathered}\]
Evaluating the boundary term at \(t=1\) and \(t=0\) (for \(m > - 1\)):
\[\begin{gathered}I(m,n)=\frac{1^{m + 1}(1 + 1)^{n} - 0}{m + 1} - \frac{n}{m + 1}\int_{0}^{1}\ t^{m + 1}(1 + t)^{n - 1}\ dt \\ I(m,n)=\frac{2^{n}}{m + 1} - \frac{n}{m + 1}I(m + 1,n - 1)\end{gathered}\]
IIT200304201Q21:
Applying the Newton--Leibniz Rule to differentiate \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}f\prime(x)=e^{- \left( x^{2} + 1 \right)^{2}} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2} + 1) - e^{- \left( x^{2} \right)^{2}} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}) \\ f\prime(x)=2x\left( e^{- \left( x^{2} + 1 \right)^{2}} - e^{- x^{4}} \right)=2xe^{- x^{4}}\left( e^{- 2x^{2} - 1} - 1 \right)\end{gathered}\]
For all real \(x\), we have \(2x^{2} + 1 \geq 1 > 0 \Longrightarrow - 2x^{2} - 1 < 0 \Longrightarrow e^{- 2x^{2} - 1} < 1\). Therefore:
\[e^{- 2x^{2} - 1} - 1 < 0\quad \text{ and }\quad e^{- x^{4}} > 0\quad \forall x \in {\mathbb{R}}\]
For \(f(x)\) to be strictly increasing, we require \(f\prime(x) > 0\):
\[2xe^{- x^{4}}\left( e^{- 2x^{2} - 1} - 1 \right) > 0 \Longleftrightarrow x < 0\]
Hence, \(f(x)\) increases in the interval \(( - \infty,0)\).

IIT200304201Q23:
First expand the product of the last two factors:
\[\left( 1 + t^{2} \right)^{12}(1 + t^{12})(1 + t^{24})=\left( 1 + t^{2} \right)^{12}\left( 1 + t^{12} + t^{24} + t^{36} \right)\]
Therefore, the coefficient of \(t^{24}\) in the entire product is the sum of:
1. Coefficient of \(t^{24}\) in \(\left( 1 + t^{2} \right)^{12} \cdot 1\): corresponds to \(\left( t^{2} \right)^{12}\), which is \(\binom{12}{12}=1\).
2. Coefficient of \(t^{12}\) in \(\left( 1 + t^{2} \right)^{12} \cdot t^{12}\): corresponds to \(\left( t^{2} \right)^{6}\), which is \(\binom{12}{6}\).
3. Coefficient of \(t^{0}\) in \(\left( 1 + t^{2} \right)^{12} \cdot t^{24}\): corresponds to \(\left( t^{2} \right)^{0}\), which is \(\binom{12}{0}=1\).
Summing these contributions:
\[\text{Coefficient of }t^{24}=1 + \binom{12}{6} + 1=\binom{12}{6} + 2\]
IIT200304201Q24:
The volume \(V\) of the parallelepiped formed by the three coterminous edge vectors \(\overrightarrow{u}=\widehat{i} + a\widehat{j} + \widehat{k}\), \(\overrightarrow{v}=\widehat{j} + a\widehat{k}\), and \(\overrightarrow{w}=a\widehat{i} + \widehat{k}\) is given by the magnitude of the scalar triple product \(\left| \left[\overrightarrow{u}\ \overrightarrow{v}\ \overrightarrow{w}\right] \right|\):
\[\begin{gathered}D(a)=\left| \begin{matrix} 1 & a & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & a \\ a & 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right|=1(1 - 0) - a(0 - a^{2}) + 1(0 - a)=a^{3} - a + 1 \\ f\prime(a)=3a^{2} - 1=0 \Longrightarrow a= \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ f\prime\prime(a)=6a\end{gathered}\]
At \(a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), we have \(f\prime\prime\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)=\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=2\sqrt{3} > 0\), and \(f\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)=1 - \frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}} > 0\).
Hence, \(V(a)\) has a strict local minimum at \(a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). (Note: In the options provided by IIT-JEE 2003, \(a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) corresponds to the local minimum of the scalar triple product polynomial \(a^{3} - a + 1 > 0\).)
IIT200304201Q25:
Write the homogeneous linear system in standard order of variables \((x,y,z)\):
\[\begin{gathered}1x + ay + 0z=0 \\ 0x + 1y + az=0 \\ ax + 0y + 1z=0\end{gathered}\]
For a homogeneous system of linear equations to have infinitely many (non-trivial) solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must vanish (\(\Delta=0\)):
\[\Delta=\left| \begin{matrix} 1 & a & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & a \\ a & 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right|=1(1 - 0) - a(0 - a^{2}) + 0=1 + a^{3}=0\]
Solving for real \(a\):
\[a^{3}= - 1 \Longrightarrow a= - 1\]
IIT200304201Q26:
Divide the given first-order linear differential equation by \((1 + t)\):
\[\frac{dy}{dt} - \left( \frac{t}{1 + t} \right)y=\frac{1}{1 + t}\]
Step 1: Compute the Integrating Factor (I.F.):
\[\text{I}.\text{F}.=\exp \left( \int_{}^{}\ - \frac{t}{1 + t}\ dt \right)=\exp \left( \int_{}^{}\ \left( - 1 + \frac{1}{1 + t} \right)dt \right)=e^{- t + \ln |1 + t|}=(1 + t)e^{- t}\]
Step 2: Multiply by the Integrating Factor and integrate:
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[ y(t)(1 + t)e^{- t} \right]=\frac{1}{1 + t} \cdot (1 + t)e^{- t}=e^{- t}\]
Integrating both sides with respect to \(t\):
\[y(t)(1 + t)e^{- t}=\int_{}^{}\ e^{- t}\ dt= - e^{- t} + C\]
Step 3: Apply the initial condition \(y(0)= - 1\):
At \(t=0\):
\[( - 1)(1 + 0)e^{0}= - e^{0} + C \Longrightarrow - 1= - 1 + C \Longrightarrow C=0\]
Thus, \((1 + t)e^{- t}y(t)= - e^{- t} \Longrightarrow y(t)= - \frac{1}{1 + t}\). Evaluating at \(t=1\):
\[y(1)= - \frac{1}{1 + 1}= - \frac{1}{2}\]

The equation of the tangent to the ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{27} + \frac{y^{2}}{1}=1\) at the point \(P\left(3\sqrt{3}\cos \theta,\sin \theta\right)\) is:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{x\left(3\sqrt{3}\cos \theta\right)}{27} + \frac{y\sin \theta}{1}=1 \Longrightarrow \frac{x}{3\sqrt{3}\sec \theta} + \frac{y}{\csc \theta}=1 \\ S(\theta)=3\sqrt{3}\sec \theta + \csc \theta \\ S\prime(\theta)=3\sqrt{3}\sec \theta\tan \theta - \csc \theta\cot \theta=0 \\ \frac{3\sqrt{3}\sin \theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}=\frac{\cos \theta}{\sin^{2}\theta} \Longrightarrow \tan^{3}\theta=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}=\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)^{3} \Longrightarrow \tan \theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{gathered}\]
Since \(\theta \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right)\), we get \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\).

Let the vertices of the triangle be \(O(0,0)\), \(A(4,0)\), and \(B(3,4)\).
1. Altitude from \(B(3,4)\) perpendicular to side \(OA\):
Since side \(OA\) lies along the \(x\)-axis (\(y=0\)), the altitude from \(B(3,4)\) perpendicular to \(OA\) is the vertical line:
\[x=3\quad \text{--- (1)}\]
2. Altitude from \(A(4,0)\) perpendicular to side \(OB\):
The slope of side \(OB\) joining \((0,0)\) and \((3,4)\) is \(m_{OB}=\frac{4 - 0}{3 - 0}=\frac{4}{3}\).
Therefore, the slope of the altitude perpendicular to \(OB\) is \(- \frac{3}{4}\).
Passing through \(A(4,0)\), its equation is:
\[y - 0= - \frac{3}{4}(x - 4)\quad \text{--- (2)}\]
Substituting \(x=3\) from (1) into (2):
\[y= - \frac{3}{4}(3 - 4)=\frac{3}{4}\]
Thus, the orthocentre of \(\triangle OAB\) is \(H\left( 3,\frac{3}{4} \right)\).

IIT200305250Q01:
Using the property \(|w|^{2}=w\overline{w}\) for any complex number \(w\), consider the difference of squares of the numerator and denominator:
\[\begin{gathered}\left| z_{1} - z_{2} \right|^{2} - \left| 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} \right|^{2}=(z_{1} - z_{2})\left({\overline{z}}_{1} - {\overline{z}}_{2}\right) - \left(1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2}\right)\left(1 - {\overline{z}}_{1}z_{2}\right) \\ \left| z_{1} - z_{2} \right|^{2} - \left| 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} \right|^{2}=\left( \left| z_{1} \right|^{2} - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} - {\overline{z}}_{1}z_{2} + \left| z_{2} \right|^{2} \right) - \left( 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} - {\overline{z}}_{1}z_{2} + \left| z_{1} \right|^{2}\left| z_{2} \right|^{2} \right) \\ \left| z_{1} - z_{2} \right|^{2} - \left| 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} \right|^{2}=\left| z_{1} \right|^{2} + \left| z_{2} \right|^{2} - 1 - \left| z_{1} \right|^{2}\left| z_{2} \right|^{2} \\ \left| z_{1} - z_{2} \right|^{2} - \left| 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} \right|^{2}=\left| z_{1} \right|^{2}\left( 1 - \left| z_{2} \right|^{2} \right) - \left( 1 - \left| z_{2} \right|^{2} \right) \\ \left| z_{1} - z_{2} \right|^{2} - \left| 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} \right|^{2}=\left( \left| z_{1} \right|^{2} - 1 \right)\left( 1 - \left| z_{2} \right|^{2} \right)\end{gathered}\]
Given that \(\left| z_{1} \right| < 1 < \left| z_{2} \right|\), we have \(\left| z_{1} \right|^{2} < 1 \Longrightarrow \left| z_{1} \right|^{2} - 1 < 0\) and \(\left| z_{2} \right|^{2} > 1 \Longrightarrow 1 - \left| z_{2} \right|^{2} < 0\).
Since the product of two strictly negative real numbers is strictly positive:
\[\begin{gathered}\left( \left| z_{1} \right|^{2} - 1 \right)\left( 1 - \left| z_{2} \right|^{2} \right) > 0 \Longrightarrow \left| z_{1} - z_{2} \right|^{2} - \left| 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} \right|^{2} > 0 \\ \Longrightarrow \left| 1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2} \right|^{2} < \left| z_{1} - z_{2} \right|^{2} \Longrightarrow \left| \frac{1 - z_{1}{\overline{z}}_{2}}{z_{1} - z_{2}} \right| < 1\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\end{gathered}\]

IIT200305250Q02.t:
{{figure}}
Rewriting the ellipse in standard form:
\[\frac{x^{2}}{6} + \frac{y^{2}}{3}=1\]
Any point on the ellipse can be parameterized as \(P\left(\sqrt{6}\cos \theta,\sqrt{3}\sin \theta\right)\).
Method 1 (Perpendicular Distance Minimization):
The perpendicular distance \(d(\theta)\) from \(P\left(\sqrt{6}\cos \theta,\sqrt{3}\sin \theta\right)\) to the line \(x + y - 7=0\) is:
\[d(\theta)=\frac{\left| \sqrt{6}\cos \theta + \sqrt{3}\sin \theta - 7 \right|}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}}}=\frac{7 - \left( \sqrt{6}\cos \theta + \sqrt{3}\sin \theta \right)}{\sqrt{2}}\]
(since \(\sqrt{6}\cos \theta + \sqrt{3}\sin \theta \leq \sqrt{6 + 3}=3 < 7\)).
Thus, \(d(\theta)\) is minimum when \(\sqrt{6}\cos \theta + \sqrt{3}\sin \theta\) is maximum, which occurs when \((\cos \theta,\sin \theta)\) is parallel to \(\left(\sqrt{6},\sqrt{3}\right)\):
\[\frac{\cos \theta}{\sqrt{6}}=\frac{\sin \theta}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6 + 3}}=\frac{1}{3} \Longrightarrow \cos \theta=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3},\quad \sin \theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\]
Substituting back into \(P\left(\sqrt{6}\cos \theta,\sqrt{3}\sin \theta\right)\):
\[x=\sqrt{6}\left( \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \right)=2,\quad y=\sqrt{3}\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \right)=1\]
Method 2 (Parallel Tangent Condition):
At the point \(P(x_{1},y_{1})\) of minimum distance, the tangent to \(x^{2} + 2y^{2}=6\) is parallel to \(x + y=7\) (slope \(= - 1\)).
Differentiating \(x^{2} + 2y^{2}=6\):
\[2x + 4y\frac{dy}{dx}=0 \Longrightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}= - \frac{x_{1}}{2y_{1}}= - 1 \Longrightarrow x_{1}=2y_{1}\]
Substituting \(x_{1}=2y_{1}\) into \(x_{1}^{2} + 2y_{1}^{2}=6\) gives \(6y_{1}^{2}=6 \Longrightarrow y_{1}= \pm 1\).
Clearly, \((2,1)\) in the first quadrant is closer to \(x + y=7\) than \(( - 2, - 1)\).
Thus, the required point is \((2,1)\).

IIT200305250Q03:
Given that \(A\) is symmetric (\(A^{T}=A\)) and orthogonal (\(A^{T}A=I\)):
\[A^{T}A=\begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ b & c & a \\ c & a & b \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ b & c & a \\ c & a & b \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} & ab + bc + ca & ab + bc + ca \\ ab + bc + ca & a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} & ab + bc + ca \\ ab + bc + ca & ab + bc + ca & a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]
Comparing the diagonal and off-diagonal entries:
\[a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}=1\quad \text{ and }\quad ab + bc + ca=0\]
Using the algebraic identity \((a + b + c)^{2}=a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} + 2(ab + bc + ca)\):
\[(a + b + c)^{2}=1 + 2(0)=1\]
Since \(a,b,c\) are given to be positive real numbers (\(a + b + c > 0\)), we have \(a + b + c=1\). Now use the identity for the sum of cubes:
\[a^{3} + b^{3} + c^{3} - 3abc=(a + b + c)\left( a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} - (ab + bc + ca) \right)\]
Substituting \(a + b + c=1\), \(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}=1\), \(ab + bc + ca=0\), and \(abc=1\):
\[a^{3} + b^{3} + c^{3} - 3(1)=(1)(1 - 0)=1 \Longrightarrow a^{3} + b^{3} + c^{3}=4\]
IIT200305250Q04:
Let \(S\) denote the left-hand side of the identity:
\[S=\sum_{r=0}^{k}\ ( - 1)^{r}2^{k - r}\binom{n}{r}\binom{n - r}{k - r}\]
Use the standard combinatorial subset-of-a-subset identity:
\[\binom{n}{r}\binom{n - r}{k - r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n - r)!} \cdot \frac{(n - r)!}{(k - r)!(n - k)!}=\frac{n!}{k!(n - k)!} \cdot \frac{k!}{r!(k - r)!}=\binom{n}{k}\binom{k}{r}\]
Substituting this identity into the summation for \(S\) and factoring \(\binom{n}{k}\) outside the sum (since it is independent of \(r\)):
\[S=\sum_{r=0}^{k}\ ( - 1)^{r}2^{k - r}\binom{n}{k}\binom{k}{r}=\binom{n}{k}\sum_{r=0}^{k}\ \binom{k}{r}2^{k - r}( - 1)^{r}\]
By the Binomial Theorem, \(\sum_{r=0}^{k}\ \binom{k}{r}2^{k - r}( - 1)^{r}=(2 - 1)^{k}=1^{k}=1\). Therefore:
\[S=\binom{n}{k} \cdot (2 - 1)^{k}=\binom{n}{k}\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]
IIT200305250Q05:
Split the integral on the left-hand side (\(I\)) at \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\):
\[\begin{gathered}I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\ f(\cos 2x)\cos x\ dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f(\cos 2x)\cos x\ dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\ f(\cos 2x)\cos x\ dx=I_{1} + I_{2} \\ I_{1}=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f\left( \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - 2t \right) \right)\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{4} - t \right)dt=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f(\sin 2t)\left( \frac{\cos t + \sin t}{\sqrt{2}} \right)dt \\ I_{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f\left( \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{2} + 2t \right) \right)\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{4} + t \right)dt=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f( - \sin 2t)\left( \frac{\cos t - \sin t}{\sqrt{2}} \right)dt \\ I=I_{1} + I_{2}=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f(\sin 2t)\left( \frac{\cos t + \sin t}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{\cos t - \sin t}{\sqrt{2}} \right)dt \\ I=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f(\sin 2t)\left( \frac{2\cos t}{\sqrt{2}} \right)dt=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ f(\sin 2x)\cos x\ dx\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\end{gathered}\]
IIT200305250Q06:
Let \(E_{1},E_{2},E_{3}\) denote the events of passing the \(1^{\text{st}},2^{\text{nd}},\) and \(3^{\text{rd}}\) exams respectively.
To qualify, the student must pass at least two out of the three exams, which occurs in the following four mutually exclusive cases:
1. Case 1 (\(E_{1}E_{2}E_{3}\) --- Passes all three exams):
• \(P(E_{1})=p\)
• Given \(E_{1}\) (passed \(1^{\text{st}}\)), probability of passing \(2^{\text{nd}}\) remains \(p\): \(P(E_{2} \mid E_{1})=p\)
• Given \(E_{1}E_{2}\) (passed \(2^{\text{nd}}\)), probability of passing \(3^{\text{rd}}\) remains \(p\): \(P(E_{3} \mid E_{1}E_{2})=p\)
\[\Longrightarrow P(E_{1}E_{2}E_{3})=p \cdot p \cdot p=p^{3}\]
2. Case 2 (\(E_{1}E_{2}{\overline{E}}_{3}\) --- Passes \(1^{\text{st}}\) and \(2^{\text{nd}}\), fails \(3^{\text{rd}}\)):
• \(P(E_{1})=p\), \(P(E_{2} \mid E_{1})=p\), and \(P\left({\overline{E}}_{3} \mid E_{1}E_{2}\right)=1 - p\)
\[\Longrightarrow P\left(E_{1}E_{2}{\overline{E}}_{3}\right)=p \cdot p \cdot (1 - p)=p^{2} - p^{3}\]
3. Case 3 (\(E_{1}{\overline{E}}_{2}E_{3}\) --- Passes \(1^{\text{st}}\), fails \(2^{\text{nd}}\), passes \(3^{\text{rd}}\)):
• \(P(E_{1})=p\), \(P\left({\overline{E}}_{2} \mid E_{1}\right)=1 - p\)
• Since he failed the \(2^{\text{nd}}\) exam, his probability of passing the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) exam is \(\frac{p}{2}\): \(P\left(E_{3} \mid E_{1}{\overline{E}}_{2}\right)=\frac{p}{2}\)
\[\Longrightarrow P\left(E_{1}{\overline{E}}_{2}E_{3}\right)=p(1 - p)\left( \frac{p}{2} \right)=\frac{p^{2} - p^{3}}{2}\]
4. Case 4 (\({\overline{E}}_{1}E_{2}E_{3}\) --- Fails \(1^{\text{st}}\), passes \(2^{\text{nd}}\) and \(3^{\text{rd}}\)):
• \(P\left({\overline{E}}_{1}\right)=1 - p\)
• Since he failed the \(1^{\text{st}}\) exam, \(P\left(E_{2} \mid {\overline{E}}_{1}\right)=\frac{p}{2}\)
• Since he passed the \(2^{\text{nd}}\) exam, his probability in the \(3^{\text{rd}}\) exam remains the same as in the \(2^{\text{nd}}\) exam (or reverts to \(p\); under the standard IIT-JEE interpretation "otherwise it remains the same as the original probability \(p\)", \(P\left(E_{3} \mid {\overline{E}}_{1}E_{2}\right)=p\)):
\[\Longrightarrow P\left({\overline{E}}_{1}E_{2}E_{3}\right)=(1 - p)\left( \frac{p}{2} \right)p=\frac{p^{2} - p^{3}}{2}\]
Summing all four mutually exclusive probabilities:
\[P(\text{Qualify})=p^{3} + (p^{2} - p^{3}) + \frac{p^{2} - p^{3}}{2} + \frac{p^{2} - p^{3}}{2}=p^{2} + (p^{2} - p^{3})=2p^{2} - p^{3}\]
(Note: If "remains the same" in Case 4 is interpreted as remaining at the previous exam's probability \(\frac{p}{2}\).
Then Case 4 has probability \((1 - p)\frac{p^{2}}{4}\), yielding \(\frac{7}{4}p^{2} - \frac{3}{4}p^{3}\).)

{{figure}}
The distance of the external point \(P(6,8)\) from the centre \(O(0,0)\) of the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2}=r^{2}\) is:
\[OP=\sqrt{6^{2} + 8^{2}}=\sqrt{36 + 64}=10\]
Let \(PA\) and \(PB\) be the two tangents drawn from \(P\) to the circle, and let \(\angle AOP=\angle BOP=\theta\), where \(\theta \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right)\).
In the right-angled triangle \(\triangle OAP\) (\(\angle OAP=90^{\circ}\)):
\[r=OA=OP\cos \theta=10\cos \theta\]
Let \(M\) be the midpoint of the chord of contact \(AB\), so \(OM\bot AB\). In right-angled \(\triangle OMA\) and \(\triangle AMP\):
\[AM=r\sin \theta=10\cos \theta\sin \theta,\quad PM=OP - OM=10 - r\cos \theta=10\left( 1 - \cos^{2}\theta \right)=10\sin^{2}\theta\]
Therefore, the area \(\Delta(\theta)\) of \(\triangle PAB\) enclosed by the tangents \(PA,PB\) and the chord of contact \(AB\) is:
\[\Delta(\theta)=\frac{1}{2} \times AB \times PM=AM \times PM=(10\cos \theta\sin \theta)(10\sin^{2}\theta)=100\sin^{3}\theta\cos \theta\]
Differentiating \(\Delta(\theta)\) with respect to \(\theta\):
\[\frac{d\Delta}{d\theta}=100\left( 3\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{4}\theta \right)=100\sin^{2}\theta\left( 3\cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta \right)=0\]
Since \(\theta \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right)\), \(\sin \theta \neq 0\), so:
\[\tan^{2}\theta=3 \Longrightarrow \tan \theta=\sqrt{3} \Longrightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{3} \Longrightarrow \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2}\]
By the first-derivative sign change (from \(+\) to \(-\) across \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\)), \(\Delta(\theta)\) is maximum at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\).
Thus, the radius \(r\) is:
\[r=10\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)=10 \times \frac{1}{2}=5\]

IIT200305250Q08:
Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there exists a complex number \(z\) satisfying \(|z| < \frac{1}{3}\) and \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\ a_{r}z^{r}=1\) with \(\left| a_{r} \right| < 2\) for all \(r=1,2,\ldots,n\).
Taking the modulus on both sides and applying the Triangle Inequality \(\left| w_{1} + w_{2} + \cdots + w_{n} \right| \leq \left| w_{1} \right| + \left| w_{2} \right| + \cdots + \left| w_{n} \right|\):
\[1=\left| \sum_{r=1}^{n}\ a_{r}z^{r} \right| \leq \sum_{r=1}^{n}\ \left| a_{r} \right||z|^{r}\]
Since \(\left| a_{r} \right| < 2\) for each \(r\) and \(|z| < \frac{1}{3}\):
\[1 < 2\sum_{r=1}^{n}\ |z|^{r} < 2\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\ |z|^{r}=\frac{2|z|}{1 - |z|}\]
Therefore, we must have:
\[\frac{2|z|}{1 - |z|} > 1 \Longrightarrow 2|z| > 1 - |z| \Longrightarrow 3|z| > 1 \Longrightarrow |z| > \frac{1}{3}\]
This directly contradicts the given hypothesis that \(|z| < \frac{1}{3}\). Hence, no such complex number \(z\) exists. \(\text{(Hence Proved)}\)
IIT200305250Q09:
Since both \(B\) and \(C\) are targeting \(A\) independently, let \(E_{B}\) be the event that \(B\) hits \(A\), and \(E_{C}\) be the event that \(C\) hits \(A\). Given:
\[\begin{gathered}P(E_{B})=\frac{1}{2} \Longrightarrow P\left({\overline{E}}_{B}\right)=1 - \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ P(E_{C})=\frac{1}{3} \Longrightarrow P\left({\overline{E}}_{C}\right)=1 - \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\end{gathered}\]
Let \(H\) be the event that \(A\) is hit (i.e., at least one of \(B\) or \(C\) hits \(A\)):
\[P(H)=P(E_{B} \cup E_{C})=1 - P\left({\overline{E}}_{B} \cap {\overline{E}}_{C}\right)=1 - \left( \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{3} \right)=1 - \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\]
The probability that \(B\) hits \(A\) and \(C\) does not is:
\[P\left(E_{B} \cap {\overline{E}}_{C}\right)=P(E_{B}) \cdot P\left({\overline{E}}_{C}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\]
By conditional probability (Bayes' Theorem), since \(\left(E_{B} \cap {\overline{E}}_{C}\right) \subset H\):
\[P\left(E_{B} \cap {\overline{E}}_{C} \mid H\right)=\frac{P\left(E_{B} \cap {\overline{E}}_{C}\right)}{P(H)}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{1}{2}\]

By definition, the left-hand derivative of \(f(x)\) at \(x= - a\) is:
\[f\prime( - a^{-})=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f( - a - h) - f( - a)}{- h}\]
Since \(f\) is an odd function on \([ - 2a,2a]\), we have \(f( - x)= - f(x)\) for all \(x \in [ - 2a,2a]\). Therefore:
\[f( - a - h)= - f(a + h)\quad \text{ and }\quad f( - a)= - f(a)\]
Substituting these into the limit expression:
\[f\prime( - a^{-})=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{- f(a + h) - ( - f(a))}{- h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}\]
For \(h > 0\) sufficiently small, \(x=a + h \in [a,2a]\). Using the given symmetry relation \(f(x)=f(2a - x)\) for \(x \in [a,2a]\):
\[f(a + h)=f(2a - (a + h))=f(a - h)\]
Substituting \(f(a + h)=f(a - h)\) into the limit:
\[f\prime( - a^{-})=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f(a - h) - f(a)}{h}= - \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f(a - h) - f(a)}{- h}= - f\prime(a^{-})\]
Since it is given that \(f\prime(a^{-})=0\), we obtain:
\[f\prime( - a^{-})= - 0=0\]

IIT200305250Q11:
At \(x=0\), \(\sin(\tan 0)=0=x\). Let \(x \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{4} \right]\).
Method 1 (Using Calculus / Monotonicity):
Consider the auxiliary function \(g(x)=\sin(\tan x) - x\) on \(\left[ 0,\frac{\pi}{4} \right]\). Differentiating with respect to \(x\):
\[g\prime(x)=\cos(\tan x)\sec^{2}x - 1=\cos(\tan x)(1 + \tan^{2}x) - 1\]
For \(x \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{4} \right]\), let \(t=\tan x \in (0,1]\). From the given inequality \(2(1 - \cos t) < t^{2}\) for \(t \neq 0\):
\[\cos t > 1 - \frac{t^{2}}{2}\]
Since \(1 + t^{2} > 0\) and \(1 - \frac{t^{2}}{2} > 0\) for \(t \in (0,1]\), multiplying both sides by \((1 + t^{2})\) yields:
\[\cos t(1 + t^{2}) > \left( 1 - \frac{t^{2}}{2} \right)(1 + t^{2})=1 + \frac{t^{2}}{2} - \frac{t^{4}}{2}=1 + \frac{t^{2}(1 - t^{2})}{2}\]
Since \(t=\tan x \in (0,1]\), we have \(1 - t^{2} \geq 0\), which implies:
\[g\prime(x)=\cos t(1 + t^{2}) - 1 > \frac{t^{2}(1 - t^{2})}{2} \geq 0\quad \forall x \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{4} \right]\]
Because \(g\prime(x) > 0\) on \(\left( 0,\frac{\pi}{4} \right]\) and \(g(0)=0\), \(g(x)\) is strictly increasing on \(\left[ 0,\frac{\pi}{4} \right]\). Therefore:
\[g(x) > g(0)=0 \Longrightarrow \sin(\tan x) > x\quad \forall x \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{4} \right]\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]
IIT200305250Q12:
Since \(a,b,c\) are in A.P., we have:
\[2b=a + c\quad \text{--- (1)}\]
Since \(a^{2},b^{2},c^{2}\) are in H.P., we have:
\[b^{2}=\frac{2a^{2}c^{2}}{a^{2} + c^{2}} \Longrightarrow b^{2}\left( a^{2} + c^{2} \right)=2a^{2}c^{2}\]
Substitute \(a^{2} + c^{2}=(a + c)^{2} - 2ac=(2b)^{2} - 2ac=4b^{2} - 2ac\) from (1):
\[b^{2}\left( 4b^{2} - 2ac \right)=2a^{2}c^{2} \Longrightarrow 4b^{4} - 2acb^{2} - 2a^{2}c^{2}=0\]
Dividing by \(2\) and factoring the quadratic in \(b^{2}\):
\[2b^{4} - acb^{2} - a^{2}c^{2}=0 \Longrightarrow \left( b^{2} - ac \right)\left( 2b^{2} + ac \right)=0\]
This gives two cases:
• Case 1 (\(b^{2}=ac\)):
Since \(b=\frac{a + c}{2}\) as well, we get \(\left( \frac{a + c}{2} \right)^{2}=ac \Longrightarrow (a - c)^{2}=0 \Longrightarrow a=c\), and hence \(a=b=c\).
• Case 2 (\(2b^{2} + ac=0\)):
Rewriting this condition gives:
\[b^{2}=a\left( - \frac{c}{2} \right)\]
which proves that \(a,b, - \frac{c}{2}\) are in Geometric Progression (G.P.). \(\text{(Hence Proved)}\)
IIT200305250Q13:
For the quadratic equation \(x^{2} + (a - b)x + (1 - a - b)=0\) in \(x\) to have unequal real roots, its discriminant \(D_{x}\) must be strictly positive (\(D_{x} > 0\)) for all \(b \in {\mathbb{R}}\):
\[\begin{gathered}D_{x}=(a - b)^{2} - 4(1)(1 - a - b) > 0\quad \forall b \in {\mathbb{R}} \\ b^{2} - 2ab + a^{2} - 4 + 4a + 4b > 0 \Longrightarrow b^{2} + 2(2 - a)b + \left( a^{2} + 4a - 4 \right) > 0\quad \forall b \in {\mathbb{R}} \\ \frac{D_{b}}{4}=(2 - a)^{2} - 1\left( a^{2} + 4a - 4 \right) < 0 \\ 4 - 4a + a^{2} - a^{2} - 4a + 4 < 0 \Longrightarrow 8 - 8a < 0 \Longrightarrow a > 1\end{gathered}\]

For the parabola \(y^{2}=4x\) (here \(a=1\)), the equation of the normal with slope \(m\) is:
\[y=mx - 2m - m^{3}\]
If this normal passes through the point \(P(h,k)\), then \(m\) satisfies the cubic equation:
\[m^{3} + (2 - h)m + k=0\quad \text{--- (1)}\]
Let the three roots of (1) be \(m_{1},m_{2},m_{3}\). By Vieta's formulas:
• \(m_{1} + m_{2} + m_{3}=0\)
• \(m_{1}m_{2} + m_{2}m_{3} + m_{3}m_{1}=2 - h\)
• \(m_{1}m_{2}m_{3}= - k\quad \text{--- (2)}\)
Given that \(m_{1}m_{2}=\alpha\), substituting into (2) gives:
\[\alpha m_{3}= - k \Longrightarrow m_{3}= - \frac{k}{\alpha}\]
Since \(m_{3}= - \frac{k}{\alpha}\) is a root of the cubic equation (1), substitute \(m= - \frac{k}{\alpha}\) into (1):
\[\left( - \frac{k}{\alpha} \right)^{3} + (2 - h)\left( - \frac{k}{\alpha} \right) + k=0\]
For \(k \neq 0\), divide through by \(k\) and multiply by \(\alpha^{3}\):
\[- k^{2} - \alpha^{2}(2 - h) + \alpha^{3}=0 \Longrightarrow k^{2}=\alpha^{2}h + \alpha^{3} - 2\alpha^{2}\]
Replacing \((h,k)\) with \((x,y)\), the locus of \(P\) is:
\[y^{2}=\alpha^{2}x + \alpha^{2}(\alpha - 2)\]
Since this locus is given to be a part of the parabola \(y^{2}=4x\) itself, comparing coefficients yields:
\[\alpha^{2}=4\quad \text{ and }\quad \alpha^{2}(\alpha - 2)=0 \Longrightarrow \alpha=2\]

IIT200305250Q15:
Proof of Part (i):
Since \(f:[0,4] \to {\mathbb{R}}\) is differentiable on \([0,4]\), it is continuous on \([0,4]\) and differentiable on \((0,4)\).
1. By Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT) on \([0,4]\), there exists \(a \in (0,4)\) such that:
\[\frac{f(4) - f(0)}{4 - 0}=f\prime(a) \Longrightarrow f(4) - f(0)=4f\prime(a)\quad \text{--- (1)}\]
2. Since \(f\) is continuous on \([0,4]\), by the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT), the arithmetic mean \(\frac{f(0) + f(4)}{2}\) lies between \(f(0)\) and \(f(4)\), so there exists \(b \in (0,4)\) such that:
\[\frac{f(4) + f(0)}{2}=f(b) \Longrightarrow f(4) + f(0)=2f(b)\quad \text{--- (2)}\]
Multiplying (1) and (2) together:
\[\left( f(4) \right)^{2} - \left( f(0) \right)^{2}=\left( f(4) - f(0) \right)\left( f(4) + f(0) \right)=4f\prime(a) \cdot 2f(b)=8f\prime(a)f(b)\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]
Proof of Part (ii):
In the integral \(I=\int_{0}^{4}\ f(t)\ dt\), substitute \(t=z^{2}\) so that \(dt=2z\ dz\). As \(t:0 \to 4\), \(z:0 \to 2\):
\[\int_{0}^{4}\ f(t)\ dt=\int_{0}^{2}\ 2zf(z^{2})\ dz\]
Define \(G(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\ 2zf(z^{2})\ dz\) on \([0,2]\).
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(G\prime(x)=2xf(x^{2})\).
Applying LMVT to \(G(x)\) on \([0,1]\) and \([1,2]\) (or IVT to the continuous function \(h(z)=2zf(z^{2})\) on \((0,1)\) and \((1,2)\)):
• On \([0,1]\), there exists \(\alpha \in (0,1) \subset (0,2)\) such that \(\int_{0}^{1}\ 2zf(z^{2})\ dz=(1 - 0) \cdot 2\alpha f(\alpha^{2})=2\alpha f(\alpha^{2})\).
• On \([1,2]\), there exists \(\beta \in (1,2) \subset (0,2)\) such that \(\int_{1}^{2}\ 2zf(z^{2})\ dz=(2 - 1) \cdot 2\beta f(\beta^{2})=2\beta f(\beta^{2})\).
Adding both integrals:
\[\int_{0}^{4}\ f(t)\ dt=2\left[ \alpha f(\alpha^{2}) + \beta f(\beta^{2}) \right]\quad \text{for some }0 < \alpha,\beta < 2\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]

Part (i): Equation of the Plane:
Let the three given points be \(A(2,1,0)\), \(B(5,0,1)\), and \(C(4,1,1)\). Two vectors lying in the plane are:
\[\begin{gathered}\overrightarrow{AB}=(5 - 2)\widehat{i} + (0 - 1)\widehat{j} + (1 - 0)\widehat{k}=3\widehat{i} - \widehat{j} + \widehat{k} \\ \overrightarrow{AC}=(4 - 2)\widehat{i} + (1 - 1)\widehat{j} + (1 - 0)\widehat{k}=2\widehat{i} + 0\widehat{j} + \widehat{k}\end{gathered}\]
The normal vector \(\overrightarrow{n}\) to the plane is given by the cross product \(\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}\):
\[\overrightarrow{n}=\left| \begin{matrix} \widehat{i} & \widehat{j} & \widehat{k} \\ 3 & - 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right|=\widehat{i}( - 1 - 0) - \widehat{j}(3 - 2) + \widehat{k}(0 - ( - 2))= - \widehat{i} - \widehat{j} + 2\widehat{k}\]
Thus, the equation of the plane passing through \(A(2,1,0)\) with normal \((1,1, - 2)\) is:
\[1(x - 2) + 1(y - 1) - 2(z - 0)=0 \Longrightarrow x + y - 2z - 3=0 \Longrightarrow x + y - 2z=3\]
Part (ii): Coordinates of the Mirror Image Point \(Q\):
Since \(PQ\) is perpendicular to the plane \(x + y - 2z - 3=0\) and the midpoint of \(PQ\) lies on the plane, \(Q(x_{2},y_{2},z_{2})\) is the reflection (mirror image) of \(P(2,1,6)\) across the plane:
\[\frac{x_{2} - 2}{1}=\frac{y_{2} - 1}{1}=\frac{z_{2} - 6}{- 2}=\frac{- 2\left( 1(2) + 1(1) - 2(6) - 3 \right)}{1^{2} + 1^{2} + ( - 2)^{2}}=\frac{- 2(2 + 1 - 12 - 3)}{6}=\frac{- 2( - 12)}{6}=4\]
Solving for \((x_{2},y_{2},z_{2})\):
\[x_{2}=2 + 4(1)=6,\quad y_{2}=1 + 4(1)=5,\quad z_{2}=6 + 4( - 2)= - 2\]
Hence, the point \(Q\) is \((6,5, - 2)\). (Check: Midpoint of \(P(2,1,6)\) and \(Q(6,5, - 2)\) is \(M(4,3,2)\), and \(4 + 3 - 2(2)=3\), which lies on the plane.)

IIT200305250Q17:
Given the differential inequality for \(x > 1\):
\[\frac{dP(x)}{dx} - P(x) > 0\quad \forall x > 1\]
Multiply both sides by the strictly positive integrating factor \(e^{- x} > 0\):
\[e^{- x}\frac{dP(x)}{dx} - e^{- x}P(x) > 0 \Longrightarrow \frac{d}{dx}\left( e^{- x}P(x) \right) > 0\quad \forall x > 1\]
Let \(F(x)=e^{- x}P(x)\). Since \(F\prime(x) > 0\) for all \(x > 1\), the function \(F(x)\) is strictly increasing on \([1,\infty)\). Therefore, for every \(x > 1\):
\[F(x) > F(1) \Longrightarrow e^{- x}P(x) > e^{- 1}P(1)\]
Since \(P(1)=0\), we have \(e^{- x}P(x) > 0\). Because \(e^{- x} > 0\) for all real \(x\), multiplying by \(e^{x} > 0\) yields:
\[P(x) > 0\quad \forall x > 1\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]

Consider a circle of radius \(R=1\). An \(n\)-sided regular polygon consists of \(n\) congruent isosceles triangles with central angle \(\frac{2\pi}{n}\).
1. Area of the inscribed regular \(n\)-gon (\(I_{n}\)):
Each of the \(n\) triangles has two sides of length \(R=1\) and included angle \(\frac{2\pi}{n}\):
\[\begin{gathered}I_{n}=n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1^{2} \cdot \sin \frac{2\pi}{n} \right)=\frac{n}{2}\sin \frac{2\pi}{n} \Longrightarrow \sin \frac{2\pi}{n}=\frac{2I_{n}}{n}\quad \text{--- (1)} \\ O_{n}=n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot 2\tan \frac{\pi}{n} \right)=n\tan \frac{\pi}{n}\quad \text{--- (2)} \\ \frac{I_{n}}{O_{n}}=\frac{\frac{n}{2}\sin \frac{2\pi}{n}}{n\tan \frac{\pi}{n}}=\frac{\frac{n}{2}\left( 2\sin \frac{\pi}{n}\cos \frac{\pi}{n} \right)}{n\frac{\sin(\pi/n)}{\cos(\pi/n)}}=\cos^{2}\frac{\pi}{n}=\frac{1 + \cos \frac{2\pi}{n}}{2} \\ \frac{I_{n}}{O_{n}}=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1 + \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}\frac{2\pi}{n}} \right)=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1 + \sqrt{1 - \left( \frac{2I_{n}}{n} \right)^{2}} \right) \\ \Longrightarrow I_{n}=\frac{O_{n}}{2}\left( 1 + \sqrt{1 - \left( \frac{2I_{n}}{n} \right)^{2}} \right)\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\end{gathered}\]

IIT200305250Q19:
Since \(\overrightarrow{u},\overrightarrow{v},\overrightarrow{w}\) are unit vectors and the angle between \(\overrightarrow{u}\) and \(\overrightarrow{v}\) is \(\alpha\), the magnitude of \(\overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}\) is:
\[\left| \overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v} \right|=\sqrt{\left| \overrightarrow{u} \right|^{2} + \left| \overrightarrow{v} \right|^{2} + 2\overrightarrow{u} \cdot \overrightarrow{v}}=\sqrt{1 + 1 + 2\cos \alpha}=\sqrt{4\cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}}=2\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}\]
Therefore, the unit vectors \(\overrightarrow{x},\overrightarrow{y},\overrightarrow{z}\) along the internal angle bisectors are:
\[\overrightarrow{x}=\frac{\overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}}{2\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}},\quad \overrightarrow{y}=\frac{\overrightarrow{v} + \overrightarrow{w}}{2\cos \frac{\beta}{2}},\quad \overrightarrow{z}=\frac{\overrightarrow{w} + \overrightarrow{u}}{2\cos \frac{\gamma}{2}}\]
Recall two standard identities of scalar triple products:
1. \(\left[ \overrightarrow{x} \times \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{y} \times \overrightarrow{z}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \times \overrightarrow{x} \right]=\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]^{2}\)
2. \(\left[ \overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{v} + \overrightarrow{w}\quad \overrightarrow{w} + \overrightarrow{u} \right]=2\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]\)
First compute \(\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]\):
\[\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]=\frac{\left[ \overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{v} + \overrightarrow{w}\quad \overrightarrow{w} + \overrightarrow{u} \right]}{8\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}\cos \frac{\beta}{2}\cos \frac{\gamma}{2}}=\frac{2\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]}{8\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}\cos \frac{\beta}{2}\cos \frac{\gamma}{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]\sec \frac{\alpha}{2}\sec \frac{\beta}{2}\sec \frac{\gamma}{2}\]
Squaring both sides yields:
\[\left[ \overrightarrow{x} \times \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{y} \times \overrightarrow{z}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \times \overrightarrow{x} \right]=\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]^{2}=\frac{1}{16}\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]^{2}\sec^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\sec^{2}\frac{\beta}{2}\sec^{2}\frac{\gamma}{2}\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]

Let \(r(t)\) and \(h(t)\) denote the radius of the top circular liquid surface and the depth of the liquid in the cone at time \(t\), respectively.
Initially at \(t=0\), the cone is full, so \(h(0)=H\) and \(r(0)=R\).
By similar triangles in the vertical cross-section of the cone:
\[\frac{r}{h}=\frac{R}{H} \Longrightarrow r=\frac{R}{H}h\]
The volume \(V(t)\) of the liquid in the cone and the surface area \(S(t)\) in contact with air at time \(t\) are:
\[V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h=\frac{1}{3}\pi\left( \frac{R}{H}h \right)^{2}h=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{3H^{2}}h^{3},\quad S=\pi r^{2}=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{H^{2}}h^{2}\]
Differentiating \(V\) with respect to time \(t\):
\[\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{3H^{2}} \cdot 3h^{2}\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{H^{2}}h^{2}\frac{dh}{dt}=S\frac{dh}{dt}\]
According to the problem statement, the liquid evaporates at a rate proportional to \(S\) with constant \(k > 0\):
\[\frac{dV}{dt}= - kS \Longrightarrow S\frac{dh}{dt}= - kS \Longrightarrow \frac{dh}{dt}= - k\]
Integrating with respect to \(t\):
\[h(t)= - kt + C\]
At \(t=0\), \(h(0)=H \Longrightarrow C=H\), so \(h(t)=H - kt\). When the cone becomes completely empty, \(h(T)=0\):
\[H - kT=0 \Longrightarrow T=\frac{H}{k}\]

IIT200504101Q01:
Let the equilateral triangle be \(\triangle ABC\) with side length \(a\), and let the centres of the two coins touching side \(BC\) be \(O_{1}\) and \(O_{2}\), each of radius \(r = 1\text{ cm}\).
• Since the circle with centre \(O_{1}\) touches two sides meeting at vertex \(B\) (where \(\angle B = 60^{\circ}\)), the line \(BO_{1}\) bisects \(\angle B\), making an angle of \(30^{\circ}\) with side \(BC\).
• Dropping a perpendicular from \(O_{1}\) to \(BC\) at the point of tangency \(P_{1}\), we have \(O_{1}P_{1} = r = 1\text{ cm}\) and \(BP_{1} = r\cot 30^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\).
• The distance between the points of tangency \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) along \(BC\) is \(P_{1}P_{2} = O_{1}O_{2} = 2r = 2\text{ cm}\), and by symmetry \(P_{2}C = \sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\).
• Thus, the side length of the equilateral triangle is \(a = \sqrt{3} + 2 + \sqrt{3} = 2 + 2\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\), and its area is:
\[\text{Area} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\left( 2 + 2\sqrt{3} \right)^{2} = \sqrt{3}\left( 4 + 2\sqrt{3} \right) = 6 + 4\sqrt{3}{\text{ cm}}^{2}\]
IIT200504101Q02:
The curves \(y = (x - 1)^{2}\) and \(y = (x + 1)^{2}\) are symmetric about the y-axis and intersect at \((0,1)\).
For \(x \geq 0\), setting \((x - 1)^{2} = \frac{1}{4}\) on the inner branch gives \(x = \frac{1}{2}\).
By symmetry:
\[\text{Area} = 2\int_{0}^{1/2}{}\left[ (x - 1)^{2} - \frac{1}{4} \right] dx = 2\left[ \frac{(x - 1)^{3}}{3} - \frac{x}{4} \right]_{0}^{1/2} = 2\left[ \left( - \frac{1}{24} - \frac{1}{8} \right) - \left( - \frac{1}{3} \right) \right] = \frac{1}{3}\]
IIT200504101Q03:
Rewriting \(x^{3} + 3x^{2} + 3x + 3 = (x + 1)^{3} + 2\) and substituting \(t = x + 1\):
\[I = \int_{- 1}^{1}{}\left( t^{3} + 2 + t\cos t \right)dt = 0 + \int_{- 1}^{1}{}2\ dt + 0 = 4\]
(since \(t^{3}\) and \(t\cos t\) are odd functions on \([ - 1,1]\)).
IIT200504101Q04:
The tangent to \(x^{2} = y - 6\) at \((1,7)\) is \(x(1) = \frac{y + 7}{2} - 6 \Longrightarrow 2x - y + 5 = 0\).
The point of contact \(P(h,k)\) is the foot of the perpendicular from the circle's centre \(C( - 8, - 6)\) onto \(2x - y + 5 = 0\):
\[\frac{h + 8}{2} = \frac{k + 6}{- 1} = - \frac{2( - 8) - ( - 6) + 5}{2^{2} + ( - 1)^{2}} = 1 \Longrightarrow (h,k) = ( - 6, - 7)\]
IIT200504101Q05:
Writing \(\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{x}\) and putting \(x = vy \Longrightarrow \frac{dx}{dy} = v + y\frac{dv}{dy}\):
\[y\frac{dv}{dy} = \frac{1}{v} \Longrightarrow \int_{}^{}{}v\ dv = \int_{}^{}{}\frac{dy}{y} \Longrightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{2y^{2}} = \ln|y| + C\]
Using \(y(1) = 1 \Longrightarrow C = \frac{1}{2}\). For \(y(x_{0}) = e\):
\[\frac{x_{0}^{2}}{2e^{2}} = \ln e + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2} \Longrightarrow x_{0} = \pm e\sqrt{3}\]
IIT200504101Q06:
Let the centre be \((h,k)\), so its radius is \(|k|\). Since it touches \(x^{2} + (y - 1)^{2} = 1\) externally:
\[\sqrt{h^{2} + (k - 1)^{2}} = |k| + 1 \Longrightarrow h^{2} + k^{2} - 2k + 1 = k^{2} + 2|k| + 1 \Longrightarrow h^{2} = 2(k + |k|)\]
For \(k \geq 0\), \(h^{2} = 4k\); for \(k < 0\), \(h = 0\). Hence the locus is \(\{ x^{2} = 4y\} \cup \{(0,y),y < 0\}\).
IIT200504101Q07:

IIT200504101Q09:
The centroid of \(\triangle ABC\) is \((x,y,z) = \left( \frac{a}{3},\frac{b}{3},\frac{c}{3} \right)\). Since the plane is at a unit distance from the origin:
\[\frac{1}{a^{2}} + \frac{1}{b^{2}} + \frac{1}{c^{2}} = 1 \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{9x^{2}} + \frac{1}{9y^{2}} + \frac{1}{9z^{2}} = 1 \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{x^{2}} + \frac{1}{y^{2}} + \frac{1}{z^{2}} = 9 \Longrightarrow K = 9\]
IIT200504101Q10:

IIT200504101Q13:

IIT200505220Q01:
Let \(C,S,B,T\) be the events of the person going by car, scooter, bus, or train, respectively:
\[P(C) = \frac{1}{7},\quad P(S) = \frac{3}{7},\quad P(B) = \frac{2}{7},\quad P(T) = \frac{1}{7}\]
Let \(\overline{L}\) be the event of the person reaching the office in time. Then:
\[P\left(\overline{L}|C\right) = \frac{7}{9},\quad P\left(\overline{L}|S\right) = \frac{8}{9},\quad P\left(\overline{L}|B\right) = \frac{5}{9},\quad P\left(\overline{L}|T\right) = \frac{8}{9}\]
By Bayes' theorem:
\[P\left(C|\overline{L}\right) = \frac{P(C)P\left(\overline{L}|C\right)}{P\left(\overline{L}\right)} = \frac{\frac{1}{7} \times \frac{7}{9}}{\frac{1}{7} \times \frac{7}{9} + \frac{3}{7} \times \frac{8}{9} + \frac{2}{7} \times \frac{5}{9} + \frac{1}{7} \times \frac{8}{9}} = \frac{7}{7 + 24 + 10 + 8} = \frac{1}{7}\]

Let \(A,B,C\) be the centres of the three circles with radii \(3,4,5\).
Then the sides of \(\triangle ABC\) are \(c = AB = 3 + 4 = 7\), \(a = BC = 4 + 5 = 9\), and \(b = CA = 5 + 3 = 8\).
Clearly, the point \(P\) (the radical centre where the common internal tangents meet) is the incentre of \(\triangle ABC\), and its distance from the points of contact equals the inradius \(r\) of \(\triangle ABC\):
\[\begin{gathered}2s = 7 + 8 + 9 = 24 \Longrightarrow s = 12 \\ r = \frac{\Delta}{s} = \sqrt{\frac{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}{s}} = \sqrt{\frac{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3}{12}} = \sqrt{5}\end{gathered}\]

\[\begin{gathered}(3\lambda + 2)x + (\lambda - 1)y + (\lambda + 1)z - 5\lambda - 3 = 0 \\ \left| \frac{6\lambda + 4 + \lambda - 1 - \lambda - 1 - 5\lambda - 3}{\sqrt{(3\lambda + 2)^{2} + (\lambda - 1)^{2} + (\lambda + 1)^{2}}} \right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \Longrightarrow 6(\lambda - 1)^{2} = 11\lambda^{2} + 12\lambda + 6 \\ \Longrightarrow 5\lambda^{2} + 24\lambda = 0 \Longrightarrow \lambda = 0\ \text{ or }\ \lambda = - \frac{24}{5}\end{gathered}\]

IIT200505220Q05:

\[\lim\limits_{x_{1} \to x_{2}}\left| \frac{f(x_{1}) - f(x_{2})}{x_{1} - x_{2}} \right| \leq \lim\limits_{x_{1} \to x_{2}}|x_{1} - x_{2}| = 0 \Longrightarrow f'(x) = 0\quad \forall x \in {\mathbb{R}}\]
Hence \(f(x)\) is a constant function. Since \(P(1,2)\) lies on the curve, \(f(x) = 2\), and the equation of the tangent is \(y - 2 = 0\).
IIT200505220Q06:
Summing the arithmetico-geometric progression (AGP):
\[S_{n} = \sum_{k = 1}^{n}{}k \cdot 2^{n + 1 - k} = 2^{n + 1}\sum_{k = 1}^{n}{}k \cdot 2^{- k} = 2^{n + 1} \cdot 2\left[ 1 - \frac{1}{2^{n}} - \frac{n}{2^{n + 1}} \right] = 2\left( 2^{n + 1} - 2 - n \right)\]
Equating to \(\left( \frac{n + 1}{4} \right)(2^{n + 1} - n - 2)\):
\[\frac{n + 1}{4} = 2 \Longrightarrow n = 7\]

IIT200505220Q10:
Any point on the hyperbola \(\frac{x^{2}}{9} - \frac{y^{2}}{4} = 1\) is \((3\sec\theta,2\tan\theta)\). Its chord of contact with respect to \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 9\) is:
\[3x\sec\theta + 2y\tan\theta = 9\]
If \((x_{1},y_{1})\) is the midpoint of the chord of contact, its equation is also \(xx_{1} + yy_{1} = x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2}\). Comparing coefficients:
\[\frac{3\sec\theta}{x_{1}} = \frac{2\tan\theta}{y_{1}} = \frac{9}{x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2}} \Longrightarrow \sec\theta = \frac{3x_{1}}{x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2}},\quad \tan\theta = \frac{9y_{1}}{2(x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2})}\]
Using \(\sec^{2}\theta - \tan^{2}\theta = 1\), the required locus is:
\[\frac{x^{2}}{9} - \frac{y^{2}}{4} = \left( \frac{x^{2} + y^{2}}{9} \right)^{2}\]
IIT200505220Q11:

\[y = - \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}x + 4\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}\]
It meets the coordinate axes at \(A\left(2\sqrt{7},0\right)\) and \(B\left( 0,4\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}} \right)\), so the intercept length is:

IIT200505220Q15:
Putting \(x = y\) in \(f(x - y) = f(x)g(y) - f(y)g(x)\) gives \(f(0) = 0\). Putting \(y = 0\) gives \(g(0) = 1\), and \(f( - h) = - f(h)\).
Thus \(f'(0^{+}) = \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f(h)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f( - h)}{- h} = f'(0^{-})\), so \(f(x)\) is differentiable at \(x = 0\).
Putting \(y = x\) in \(g(x - y) = g(x)g(y) + f(x)f(y)\) gives:
\[f^{2}(x) + g^{2}(x) = g(0) = 1 \Longrightarrow 2g(0)g'(0) = - 2f(0)f'(0) = 0 \Longrightarrow g'(0) = 0\]
IIT200505220Q16:
Let \(P(x) = ax^{3} + bx^{2} + cx + d\). From the given conditions:
\[\begin{gathered}P( - 1) = - a + b - c + d = 10,\quad P(1) = a + b + c + d = - 6 \\ P'( - 1) = 3a - 2b + c = 0,\quad P''(1) = 6a + 2b = 0 \Longrightarrow b = - 3a\end{gathered}\]
Solving for \(a,b,c,d\) gives \(a = 1,b = - 3,c = - 9,d = 5\), so:
\[P(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 9x + 5,\quad P'(x) = 3(x + 1)(x - 3)\]
Thus \(x = - 1\) gives the local maximum \(( - 1,10)\) and \(x = 3\) gives the local minimum \((3, - 22)\). The distance between them is:
\[\sqrt{(3 - ( - 1))^{2} + ( - 22 - 10)^{2}} = \sqrt{16 + 1024} = 4\sqrt{65}\ \text{units}\]

IIT200505220Q17.t:
From \(f'(x) = g(x)\) and \(|f(x)| \leq 1\):
\[\begin{gathered}\left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| = |f(3) - f(0)| \leq 2\quad \text{ and }\quad \left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| = |f(0) - f( - 3)| \leq 2 \\ \Longrightarrow \left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| + \left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| \leq 4\quad \ldots(1)\end{gathered}\]
Also, from \(f^{2}(0) + g^{2}(0) = 9\) and \(|f(0)| \leq 1\), we have \(2\sqrt{2} \leq |g(0)| \leq 3\).
{{figure}}
• Case I (\(2\sqrt{2} \leq g(0) \leq 3\)): Suppose \(g(x)\) is concave upward (\(g''(x) > 0\)) for all \(x \in ( - 3,3)\) and \(g(x) > 0\).
Then the tangent line to \(y = g(x)\) at \((0,g(0))\) lies below the curve, so the sum of areas satisfies:
\[\left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| + \left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| \geq 6g(0) \geq 12\sqrt{2} > 4\]
(or at least \(3g(0) \geq 6\sqrt{2} > 4\) on one of the half-intervals \([ - 3,0]\) or \([ 0,3]\) depending on the sign of \(g'(0)\)), which contradicts \((1)\).
Hence \(g''(c) < 0\) at some point \(c \in ( - 3,3)\) where \(g(c) \geq 2\sqrt{2} > 0\), giving \(g(c)g''(c) < 0\).
• Case II (\(- 3 \leq g(0) \leq - 2\sqrt{2}\)): Similarly, if \(g(x)\) were concave downward (\(g''(x) < 0\)) across the region where \(g(x) < 0\).
Then \(\left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| + \left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| > 6\sqrt{2} > 4\), contradicting \((1)\).
Thus \(g''(c) > 0\) at some point \(c \in ( - 3,3)\) where \(g(c) \leq - 2\sqrt{2} < 0\), so \(g(c)g''(c) < 0\).
Hence, there exists \(c \in ( - 3,3)\) such that \(g(c)g''(c) < 0\).
