BB-26-3-013:
Step 1: Compute \(\overset{\rightarrow}{GE} = \overset{\rightarrow}{e} - \overset{\rightarrow}{g}\) using \(\overset{\rightarrow}{e} = \frac{3\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + 2\overset{\rightarrow}{c}}{6}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{g} = \frac{\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + \overset{\rightarrow}{c}}{3}\):
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{GE} = \frac{3\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + 2\overset{\rightarrow}{c} - 2\left( \overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \right)}{6} = \frac{\overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}}{6}\]
Step 2: Since \(\overset{\rightarrow}{GE}\bot\overset{\rightarrow}{CD}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{GE} = \frac{1}{6}\overset{\rightarrow}{BA}\), the median \(CD\) is perpendicular to the base \(AB\).
Step 3: Because the median \(CD\) through \(C\) is also the altitude through \(C\), \(\Delta ABC\) is isosceles with \(CA = CB\), and its orthocentre lies on the altitude/median \(CD\) through \(C\). Therefore, option (b) is correct.
BB-26-3-014:
Step 1: Recall that for any two vectors \(\overset{\rightarrow}{u}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{v}\), \(\left[ \overset{\rightarrow}{u}\ \overset{\rightarrow}{v}\ \left( \overset{\rightarrow}{u} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{v} \right) \right] = \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{u} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{v} \right|^{2}\). Thus the given equation is:
\[\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \right|^{2} = \lambda\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{AE} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{AG} \right|^{2}\]
Step 2: Express \(\overset{\rightarrow}{AE}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{AG}\) in terms of \(\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}\):
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{AE} = \frac{\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} + \overset{\rightarrow}{AD}}{3} = \frac{\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} + 2\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}}{6},\ \ \overset{\rightarrow}{AG} = \frac{\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} + \overset{\rightarrow}{AC}}{3}\]
Step 3: Compute \(\overset{\rightarrow}{AE} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{AG}\):
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{AE} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{AG} = \frac{1}{18}\left( \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} + 2\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \right) \times \left( \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} + \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \right) = - \frac{1}{18}\left( \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \right) \Rightarrow \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{AE} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{AG} \right|^{2} = \frac{1}{324}\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \right|^{2}\]
Hence \(\lambda = 324\). Therefore, option (d) is correct.
BB-26-3-015:
Step 1: Since the centroid (centre) of tetrahedron \(D - ABC\) is \(\frac{\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + \overset{\rightarrow}{c} + \overset{\rightarrow}{d}}{4} = \left( \frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{4},2 \right)\), find the coordinates of vertex \(D\):
\[D = 4\left( \frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{4},2 \right) - (1,1,1) - (1,2,3) - (1,1,2) = (6 - 3,3 - 4,8 - 6) = (3, - 1,2)\]
Step 2: Find the direction vectors of lines \(AB\) and \(CD\), and their cross product:
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = (0,1,2),\ \ \overset{\rightarrow}{CD} = (2, - 2,0),\ \ \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{CD} = \left| \begin{matrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & - 2 & 0 \end{matrix} \right| = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k} = 2\left( 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k} \right)\]
Step 3: Compute the shortest distance between \(AB\) (through \(A(1,1,1)\)) and \(CD\) (through \(C(1,1,2)\)), where \(\overset{\rightarrow}{AC} = (0,0,1)\):
\[S.D. = \frac{\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \cdot \left( 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k} \right) \right|}{\left| 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k} \right|} = \frac{|0 + 0 - 1|}{\sqrt{4 + 4 + 1}} = \frac{1}{3}\]
Therefore, option (b) is correct.
BB-26-3-016:
Step 1: Observe the coordinates of the three vertices of face \(ABC\): \(A(1,1,1),B(1,2,3),\) and \(C(1,1,2)\). All three points have \(x\)-coordinate equal to \(1\).
Step 2: Since \(A,B,C\) are non-collinear and all satisfy \(x = 1\), the equation of the plane containing face \(ABC\) is simply \(x = 1\).
Step 3: The foot of the perpendicular \(N\) from \(D(3, - 1,2)\) onto the plane \(x = 1\) retains the \(y\)- and \(z\)-coordinates of \(D\) while setting \(x = 1\), giving \(N = (1, - 1,2)\). Therefore, option (b) is correct.

BB-26-3-017.t:
Step 1: Let \(\overset{\rightarrow}{OA} = \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{OB} = \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\). From \(3OR = 2RB\) (\(OR:RB = 2:3\)) and \(2AQ = 3QB\) (\(AQ:QB = 3:2\)):
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{OR} = \frac{2}{5}\overset{\rightarrow}{b},\ \ \overset{\rightarrow}{OQ} = \frac{2\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + 3\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}{5}\]
Step 2: Since \(P\) divides \(OQ\) in the ratio \(\mu:1\) and also lies on \(AR\) (dividing \(AR\) in some ratio \(1:\lambda\)):
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{OP} = \frac{\mu}{\mu + 1}\left( \frac{2\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + 3\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}{5} \right) = \frac{\lambda\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \frac{2}{5}\overset{\rightarrow}{b}}{\lambda + 1}\]
Step 3: Equate the scalar coefficients of the non-collinear vectors \(\overset{\rightarrow}{a}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{b}\):
\[\frac{2\mu}{5(\mu + 1)} = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda + 1}\ \ \text{and}\ \ \frac{3\mu}{5(\mu + 1)} = \frac{2}{5(\lambda + 1)} \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{2}{3}\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) \Rightarrow \frac{2\mu + 3\mu}{5(\mu + 1)} = \frac{\lambda + 2/5}{\lambda + 1}\]
From the second equation, \(\lambda + 1 = \frac{2(\mu + 1)}{3\mu}\), so \(\lambda = \frac{2 - \mu}{3\mu}\). Substituting into the first gives \(\frac{2\mu}{5(\mu + 1)} = \frac{2 - \mu}{2(\mu + 1)} \Rightarrow 4\mu = 10 - 5\mu \Rightarrow \mu = \frac{10}{9}\). Therefore, option (d) is correct.

BB-26-3-018:
Step 1: From Question 17, \(\mu = \frac{10}{9}\), so \(\overset{\rightarrow}{OP} = \frac{10}{19}\overset{\rightarrow}{OQ} = \frac{2}{19}\left( 2\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + 3\overset{\rightarrow}{b} \right)\). Compute the area of \(\Delta OPA\) in terms of \(\Delta = \frac{1}{2}\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \right| = \text{Area}(\Delta OAB)\):
\[\text{Area}(\Delta OPA) = \frac{1}{2}\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{OP} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{OA} \right| = \frac{1}{2}\left| \frac{2}{19}\left( 2\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + 3\overset{\rightarrow}{b} \right) \times \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \right| = \frac{6}{19}\left( \frac{1}{2}\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \right| \right) = \frac{6}{19}\Delta\]

\[\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{BC} \right|^{2} + \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{DA} \right|^{2} - \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} \right|^{2} - \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{CD} \right|^{2} = \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{c} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \right|^{2} + \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{d} \right|^{2} - \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \right|^{2} - \left| \overset{\rightarrow}{d} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \right|^{2} = 2\overset{\rightarrow}{c} \cdot \left( \overset{\rightarrow}{d} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \right) = 2\left( \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{BD} \right)\]
Step 3: Substitute \(\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{AB} \right| = 3,\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{BC} \right| = 7,\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{CD} \right| = 11,\) and \(\left| \overset{\rightarrow}{DA} \right| = 9\):
\[2\left( \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{BD} \right) = \left( 7^{2} + 9^{2} \right) - \left( 3^{2} + 11^{2} \right) = (49 + 81) - (9 + 121) = 130 - 130 = 0 \Rightarrow \overset{\rightarrow}{AC} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{BD} = 0\]
BB-26-5-013:
Step 1: Recall that for a regular tetrahedron of edge length \(a\), the area of its equilateral base is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^{2}\) and its height is \(h = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}a\).
Step 2: Thus the volume \(V\) of a regular tetrahedron of unit edge length (\(a = 1\)) is:

IIT200004111Q01:
Applying the sum-to-product identity \(\sin A + \sin B = 2\sin \left( \frac{A + B}{2} \right)\cos \left( \frac{A - B}{2} \right)\) to \(\sin 3\theta + \sin \theta\), we obtain:
\[f(\theta) = \sin \theta \cdot \left( 2\sin 2\theta\cos \theta \right)\]
Rearranging the factors and using the double-angle formula \(2\sin \theta\cos \theta = \sin 2\theta\):
\[f(\theta) = (2\sin \theta\cos \theta)\sin 2\theta = (\sin 2\theta)(\sin 2\theta) = \sin ^{2}2\theta\]
Since the square of any real number is non-negative, \(\sin ^{2}2\theta \geq 0\) for every \(\theta \in {\mathbb{R}}\). Thus, \(f(\theta) \geq 0\) for all real \(\theta\), which corresponds to option (C).

IIT200004111Q02.t:
Comparing the given parabola \(y^{2} = 12x\) with the standard form \(y^{2} = 4ax\), we get \(4a = 12 \Rightarrow a = 3\).
The standard equation of a normal with slope \(m\) to the parabola \(y^{2} = 4ax\) is:
\[y = mx - 2am - am^{3}\]
Rewriting the given normal line \(x + y = k\) in slope-intercept form gives:
\[y = - x + k\]
Comparing this with the standard normal equation, the slope is \(m = - 1\) and the \(y\)-intercept is \(k = - 2am - am^{3}\). Substituting \(a = 3\) and \(m = - 1\):
\[k = - 2(3)( - 1) - (3)( - 1)^{3} = 6 + 3 = 9\]
The foot of the normal on the parabola is \((am^{2}, - 2am) = (3( - 1)^{2}, - 2(3)( - 1)) = (3,6)\). Thus \(k = 9\), which corresponds to option (B).

IIT200004111Q03:
Splitting the middle term \(2\dbinom{n}{r - 1} = \dbinom{n}{r - 1} + \dbinom{n}{r - 1}\) and grouping adjacent binomial coefficients:
\[\dbinom{n}{r} + 2\dbinom{n}{r - 1} + \dbinom{n}{r - 2} = \left[ \dbinom{n}{r} + \dbinom{n}{r - 1} \right] + \left[ \dbinom{n}{r - 1} + \dbinom{n}{r - 2} \right]\]
Applying Pascal's identity \(\dbinom{m}{k} + \dbinom{m}{k - 1} = \dbinom{m + 1}{k}\) twice:
\[= \dbinom{n + 1}{r} + \dbinom{n + 1}{r - 1} = \dbinom{n + 2}{r}\]
Hence, option (D) is correct.
IIT200004111Q04:
By Vieta's formulas for the quadratic equation \(x^{2} + bx + c = 0\):
1. Product of roots: \(\alpha\beta = c < 0\). Since the product of the roots is negative, the roots have opposite signs. Because \(\alpha < \beta\), it follows immediately that \(\alpha < 0 < \beta\).
2. Sum of roots: \(\alpha + \beta = - b < 0\) (since \(b > 0\)). Therefore:
\[\beta < - \alpha\]
Since \(\alpha < 0\), we have \(|\alpha| = - \alpha\), which gives \(\beta < |\alpha|\). Combining both inequalities yields:
\[\alpha < 0 < \beta < |\alpha|\]
Hence, option (B) is correct.
IIT200004111Q05:
Let us test each option using standard properties and counterexamples:
• (A) False: Take \(f(x) = x\), which is onto \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(g(x) = |x|\) has range \([ 0,\infty) \neq {\mathbb{R}}\), so \(g\) is not onto.
• (B) False: Take \(f(x) = x\), which is one-one on \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(g( - 1) = g(1) = 1\), so \(g\) is not one-one.
• (C) True: The absolute value function \(h(t) = |t|\) is continuous everywhere on \(\mathbb{R}\). Since the composition of two continuous functions is always continuous, if \(f\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\), then \(g(x) = (h \circ f)(x) = |f(x)|\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\).
• (D) False: Take \(f(x) = x\), which is differentiable everywhere. Then \(g(x) = |x|\) is not differentiable at \(x = 0\).
Hence, option (C) is correct.
IIT200004111Q06:
Solving the given equation \(2^{x} + 2^{y} = 2\) for \(2^{y}\):
\[2^{y} = 2 - 2^{x}\]
For \(y\) to be a well-defined real number, the exponential term \(2^{y}\) must be strictly positive (\(2^{y} > 0\) for all \(y \in {\mathbb{R}}\)):
\[2 - 2^{x} > 0 \Rightarrow 2^{x} < 2^{1}\]
Since the base \(2 > 1\), the exponential function \(2^{x}\) is strictly increasing, so:
\[x < 1 \Leftrightarrow - \infty < x < 1\]
Taking base-\(2\) logarithms gives \(y(x) = \log _{2}(2 - 2^{x})\), which is defined for all \(x \in ( - \infty,1)\). Hence, option (D) is correct.
IIT200004111Q07:
Differentiating both sides of \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 1\) with respect to \(x\):
\[2x + 2yy' = 0 \Rightarrow x + yy' = 0\]
Differentiating a second time with respect to \(x\) using the product rule on \(yy'\):
\[\begin{gathered} \frac{d}{dx}(x) + \frac{d}{dx}(yy') = 0 \Rightarrow 1 + y \cdot y'' + y' \cdot y' = 0 \\ yy'' + (y')^{2} + 1 = 0 \end{gathered}\]
Hence, option (B) is correct.
IIT200004111Q08:
Let \(X = a + b\) and \(Y = c + d\). Since \(a,b,c,d > 0\), both \(X > 0\) and \(Y > 0\), and \(X + Y = 2\).
Thus \(M = XY > 0\). By the Arithmetic Mean--Geometric Mean (AM-GM) inequality applied to the positive reals \(X\) and \(Y\):
\[\sqrt{XY} \leq \frac{X + Y}{2} \Rightarrow XY \leq \left( \frac{X + Y}{2} \right)^{2} = \left( \frac{2}{2} \right)^{2} = 1\]
Equality \(M = 1\) holds when \(a + b = c + d = 1\) (for example, \(a = b = c = d = \frac{1}{2}\)), and as \(a + b \rightarrow 0^{+}\), \(M \rightarrow 0^{+}\). Therefore, \(M\) satisfies \(0 < M \leq 1\), which lies within \(0 \leq M \leq 1\). Hence, option (A) is correct.
IIT200004111Q09:
A homogeneous system of three linear equations \(AX = 0\) has a non-trivial (non-zero) solution if and only if the determinant of its coefficient matrix vanishes (\(\det (A) = 0\)):
\[\left| \begin{matrix} 1 & - k & - 1 \\ k & - 1 & - 1 \\ 1 & 1 & - 1 \end{matrix} \right| = 0\]
Subtracting Row 3 from Row 1 (\(R_{1} \rightarrow R_{1} - R_{3}\)) and Row 3 from Row 2 (\(R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2} - R_{3}\)):
\[\left| \begin{matrix} 0 & - (k + 1) & 0 \\ k - 1 & - 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & - 1 \end{matrix} \right| = 0\]
Expanding along the third column gives:
\[( - 1)\left[ 0 - ( - (k + 1)(k - 1)) \right] = 0 \Rightarrow - (k^{2} - 1) = 0 \Rightarrow k^{2} = 1 \Rightarrow k = - 1,1\]
Hence, option (D) is correct.

IIT200004111Q10.t:

The slope of radius \(OQ\) joining \(O(0,0)\) and \(Q(3,4)\) is:

By the Inscribed Angle Theorem, the angle subtended by chord \(QR\) at a point \(P\) on the major arc of the circle is half the central angle:

IIT200004111Q11:
In \(\triangle ABC\), the sum of interior angles is \(A + B + C = \pi\), so \(A + C = \pi - B\). Substituting this into the argument of the sine function:
\[\frac{1}{2}(A - B + C) = \frac{1}{2}(\pi - 2B) = \frac{\pi}{2} - B\]
Therefore:
\[2ac\sin \left( \frac{1}{2}(A - B + C) \right) = 2ac\sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - B \right) = 2ac\cos B\]
By the Law of Cosines in \(\triangle ABC\), \(\cos B = \frac{c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2}}{2ca}\), which immediately gives:
\[2ac\cos B = c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2}\]
Hence, option (B) is correct.
IIT200004111Q12:
As \(x \rightarrow \infty\), the base \(\frac{x - 3}{x + 2} \rightarrow 1\) and the exponent \(x \rightarrow \infty\), which is of the indeterminate form \(1^{\infty}\). Using the standard limit formula \(\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty}[ f(x)]^{g(x)} = \exp \left( \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty}g(x)[ f(x) - 1] \right)\):
\[\begin{gathered} L = \exp \left( \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty}x\left( \frac{x - 3}{x + 2} - 1 \right) \right) = \exp \left( \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty}x\left( \frac{x - 3 - x - 2}{x + 2} \right) \right) \\ L = \exp \left( \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty}\frac{- 5x}{x + 2} \right) = \exp \left( \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty}\frac{- 5}{1 + \frac{2}{x}} \right) = e^{- 5} \end{gathered}\]
Hence, option (C) is correct.
IIT200004111Q13:
For a convergent infinite geometric series (\(|r| < 1\)), the sum to infinity is \(S_{\infty} = \frac{a}{1 - r} = 4\), and the second term is \(T_{2} = ar = \frac{3}{4}\).
Substituting \(a = 4(1 - r)\) into \(ar = \frac{3}{4}\):
\[4(1 - r)r = \frac{3}{4} \Rightarrow 16r - 16r^{2} = 3 \Rightarrow 16r^{2} - 16r + 3 = 0\]
Factoring the quadratic equation:
\[(4r - 1)(4r - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow r = \frac{1}{4} \text{ or } r = \frac{3}{4}\]
• When \(r = \frac{1}{4}\), we get \(a = 4\left( 1 - \frac{1}{4} \right) = 3\).
• When \(r = \frac{3}{4}\), we get \(a = 4\left( 1 - \frac{3}{4} \right) = 1\).

IIT200004111Q14:
By the additivity of definite integrals over adjacent intervals:
\[g(2) = \int_{0}^{2}f(t) dt = \int_{0}^{1}f(t) dt + \int_{1}^{2}f(t) dt\]
Integrating the given bounds over \([ 0,1]\) and \([ 1,2]\) respectively:
\[\begin{gathered} \int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2} dt \leq \int_{0}^{1}f(t) dt \leq \int_{0}^{1}1 dt \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \leq \int_{0}^{1}f(t) dt \leq 1 \\ \int_{1}^{2}0 dt \leq \int_{1}^{2}f(t) dt \leq \int_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{2} dt \Rightarrow 0 \leq \int_{1}^{2}f(t) dt \leq \frac{1}{2} \end{gathered}\]
Adding the two inequalities yields:
\[\frac{1}{2} \leq g(2) \leq \frac{3}{2}\]
Since \(\left[ \frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2} \right] \subset [ 0,2)\), \(g(2)\) satisfies the inequality \(0 \leq g(2) < 2\), which corresponds to option (B).

IIT200004111Q15.t:
In a right-angled triangle \(ABC\) with \(\angle C = \frac{\pi}{2}\), the hypotenuse is \(c\):
1. The circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so the circumradius is \(R = \frac{c}{2} \Rightarrow 2R = c\).
2. The inradius of a right-angled triangle is given by \(r = \frac{a + b - c}{2}\) (which follows from \(\Delta = \frac{1}{2}ab\), \(s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}\), and \(a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}\), since \((s - a)(s - b) = \frac{(c - (a - b))(c + (a - b))}{4} = \frac{c^{2} - a^{2} - b^{2} + 2ab}{4} = \frac{ab}{2} = \Delta = rs - r(a + b) \Rightarrow r = s - c = \frac{a + b - c}{2}\)). Thus \(2r = a + b - c\).
Adding the two relations:
\[2(r + R) = 2r + 2R = (a + b - c) + c = a + b\]
Hence, option (A) is correct.

IIT200004111Q16:
In a \(9\)-digit number, the positions from left to right are \(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\):
• There are \(4\) even positions (\(2\text{nd},4\text{th},6\text{th},8\text{th}\)) and \(5\) odd positions (\(1\text{st},3\text{rd},5\text{th},7\text{th},9\text{th}\)).
• The given digits of \(223355888\) consist of \(4\) odd digits (\(3,3,5,5\)) and \(5\) even digits (\(2,2,8,8,8\)).
1. Number of ways to arrange the \(4\) odd digits (\(3,3,5,5\)) in the \(4\) even positions:
\[N_{\text{odd}} = \frac{4!}{2! 2!} = \frac{24}{4} = 6\]
2. Number of ways to arrange the \(5\) even digits (\(2,2,8,8,8\)) in the \(5\) remaining odd positions:
\[N_{\text{even}} = \frac{5!}{2! 3!} = \frac{120}{12} = 10\]
By the fundamental principle of counting, the total number of distinct \(9\)-digit numbers is:
\[N = N_{\text{odd}} \times N_{\text{even}} = 6 \times 10 = 60\]
Hence, option (C) is correct.
IIT200004111Q17:
Let \(\theta = \arg (z)\) denote the principal argument of \(z\), which lies in \(( - \pi,\pi]\). Since \(\arg (z) < 0\), we have \(- \pi < \theta < 0\) (meaning \(z\) lies in the third or fourth quadrant).
Writing \(z = re^{i\theta}\) with \(r = |z| > 0\), the negation \(- z\) is obtained by rotating \(z\) counterclockwise by \(\pi\) radians:
\[- z = re^{i(\theta + \pi)}\]
Because \(- \pi < \theta < 0\), the angle \(\theta + \pi\) satisfies \(0 < \theta + \pi < \pi\), which lies strictly inside the principal range \(( - \pi,\pi]\). Therefore, the principal argument of \(- z\) is:
\[\arg ( - z) = \theta + \pi\]
Subtracting \(\arg (z) = \theta\) gives:
\[\arg ( - z) - \arg (z) = (\theta + \pi) - \theta = \pi\]
Hence, option (A) is correct.

Let \(O\) be the foot of the vertical pole inside \(\triangle ABC\), let \(T\) be the top of the pole of height \(h = OT\), and let \(\alpha\) be the common angle of elevation of \(T\) from each vertex \(A,B,C\).

IIT200004111Q20:
Splitting the interval of integration \([ - 2,3]\) at \(x = 2\):
\[\int_{- 2}^{3}f(x) dx = \int_{- 2}^{2}f(x) dx + \int_{2}^{3}f(x) dx = \int_{- 2}^{2}e^{\cos x}\sin x dx + \int_{2}^{3}2 dx\]
On the symmetric interval \([ - 2,2]\), let \(h(x) = e^{\cos x}\sin x\). Since \(\cos ( - x) = \cos x\) and \(\sin ( - x) = - \sin x\), we have:
\[h( - x) = e^{\cos ( - x)}\sin ( - x) = - e^{\cos x}\sin x = - h(x)\]
Thus \(h(x)\) is an odd function on \([ - 2,2]\), which implies \(\int_{- 2}^{2}e^{\cos x}\sin x dx = 0\).
Evaluating the remaining integral over \((2,3]\):
\[\int_{2}^{3}2 dx = 2(3 - 2) = 2\]
Therefore, \(\int_{- 2}^{3}f(x) dx = 0 + 2 = 2\). Hence, option (C) is correct.

• \(\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x < 0\), so \(\sin x\) is strictly decreasing on \(\left( \frac{\pi}{2},\pi \right)\).
• \(\frac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = - \sin x < 0\), so \(\cos x\) is also strictly decreasing on \(\left( \frac{\pi}{2},\pi \right)\).
Therefore, statement \(S\) is correct.
• Analysis of Statement \(R\): A differentiable function \(f(x)\) decreases on \((a,b)\) if \(f'(x) \leq 0\) on \((a,b)\), whereas its derivative \(f'(x)\) decreases only if \(f''(x) \leq 0\) (concave down). Indeed, for \(f(x) = \cos x\) on \(\left( \frac{\pi}{2},\pi \right)\), \(f\) is decreasing, but its derivative \(f'(x) = - \sin x\) has derivative \(f''(x) = - \cos x > 0\), meaning \(f'(x)\) is increasing on \(\left( \frac{\pi}{2},\pi \right)\). Thus, statement \(R\) is wrong.
Hence, option (D) is correct.
IIT200004111Q23:
By the definition of an indefinite integral, differentiating \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\) yields:
\[f'(x) = e^{x}(x - 1)(x - 2)\]
For \(f(x)\) to decrease, we require \(f'(x) \leq 0\). Since \(e^{x} > 0\) for all \(x \in {\mathbb{R}}\), the sign of \(f'(x)\) is determined entirely by the quadratic factor \((x - 1)(x - 2)\):
\[(x - 1)(x - 2) \leq 0 \Leftrightarrow x \in [ 1,2]\]
Thus, \(f\) decreases in the open interval \((1,2)\), which corresponds to option (C).
IIT200004111Q24:
Comparing the two circles with the general form \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 2g_{i}x + 2f_{i}y + c_{i} = 0\):
• First circle: \(g_{1} = 1, f_{1} = k, c_{1} = 6\).
• Second circle: \(g_{2} = 0, f_{2} = k, c_{2} = k\).
Two circles intersect orthogonally if and only if \(2g_{1}g_{2} + 2f_{1}f_{2} = c_{1} + c_{2}\):
\[2(1)(0) + 2(k)(k) = 6 + k \Rightarrow 2k^{2} - k - 6 = 0\]
Factoring the quadratic equation:
\[(2k + 3)(k - 2) = 0 \Rightarrow k = 2 \text{ or } k = - \frac{3}{2}\]
Hence, option (A) is correct.
IIT200004111Q25:
Since the directed sides \(\overset{\rightarrow}{BC} = \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\), \(\overset{\rightarrow}{CA} = \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\), and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{AB} = \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\) form a closed triangle Loop \(BC \rightarrow CA \rightarrow AB\):
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + \overset{\rightarrow}{c} = \overset{\rightarrow}{0}\]
Taking the cross product of both sides with \(\overset{\rightarrow}{a}\) on the left:
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right) = \overset{\rightarrow}{0} \Rightarrow \overset{\rightarrow}{0} + \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{c} = \overset{\rightarrow}{0} \Rightarrow \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b} = - \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{c} = \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\]
Similarly, taking the cross product of \(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} + \overset{\rightarrow}{c} = \overset{\rightarrow}{0}\) with \(\overset{\rightarrow}{b}\) on the left gives:
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{b} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{a} + \overset{\rightarrow}{0} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{c} = \overset{\rightarrow}{0} \Rightarrow \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{c} = - \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{a} = \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\]
Combining both results yields \(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b} = \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{c} = \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\).Hence, option (B) is correct.
IIT200004111Q26:
The slope of the normal to the curve \(y = f(x)\) at \((3,4)\) is:
\[m_{\text{normal}} = \tan \left( \frac{3\pi}{4} \right) = - 1\]
On the other hand, in terms of the derivative \(f'(3)\) (the slope of the tangent at \(x = 3\)), the slope of the normal is:
\[m_{\text{normal}} = - \frac{1}{f'(3)}\]
Equating the two expressions:
\[- \frac{1}{f'(3)} = - 1 \Rightarrow f'(3) = 1\]
Hence, option (D) is correct.
IIT200004111Q27:
• The normal vector to plane \(P_{1}\) (spanned by \(\overset{\rightarrow}{a}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{b}\)) is \({\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{1} = \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\).
• The normal vector to plane \(P_{2}\) (spanned by \(\overset{\rightarrow}{c}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{d}\)) is \({\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{2} = \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{d}\).
We are given that:
\[{\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{1} \times {\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{2} = \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\right) \times \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{c} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{d}\right) = \overset{\rightarrow}{0}\]
Since the cross product of the two non-zero normal vectors is the zero vector, \({\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{1}\) and \({\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{2}\) are parallel (\({\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{1} \parallel {\overset{\rightarrow}{n}}_{2}\)). Because the angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals, the angle between planes \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) is \(0\). Hence, option (A) is correct.

IIT200004111Q28.t:
By the definition of a local maximum, \(f\) has a local maximum at \(x = 0\) if there exists a neighbourhood \(( - \delta,\delta)\) around \(0\) such that \(f(x) \leq f(0)\) for all \(x \in ( - \delta,\delta)\).
Choose \(\delta = 1\) (so \(x \in ( - 1,1)\)).
• At \(x = 0\), we are given \(f(0) = 1\).
• For any \(x \in ( - 1,1) \smallsetminus \{ 0\}\), we have \(0 < |x| < 1 \leq 2\), so \(f(x) = |x| < 1 = f(0)\).
Thus \(f(x) < f(0)\) for every \(x\) in the punctured neighbourhood \(( - 1,1) \smallsetminus \{ 0\}\), which proves that \(f\) attains a strict local maximum at \(x = 0\). Hence, option (A) is correct.

IIT200004111Q29:
Since \(\overset{\rightarrow}{a},\overset{\rightarrow}{b},\overset{\rightarrow}{c}\) are coplanar vectors, their scalar triple product vanishes: \(\left[\overset{\rightarrow}{a} \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right] = 0\).
Furthermore, any linear combinations of coplanar vectors lie in the same plane and are therefore also coplanar. Explicitly, using determinant expansion in the basis \(\left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a},\overset{\rightarrow}{b},\overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right)\):
\[\left[ 2\overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\quad  2\overset{\rightarrow}{b} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\quad  2\overset{\rightarrow}{c} - \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \right] = \left| \begin{matrix} 2 & - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & - 1 \\ - 1 & 0 & 2 \end{matrix} \right|\left[\overset{\rightarrow}{a} \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right] = 7 \times 0 = 0\]
Hence, option (A) is correct.
IIT200004111Q30:
Let \(f(x) = (x - a)(x - b) - 1\). Notice that \(f(x)\) is a continuous upward-opening quadratic polynomial (\(\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \pm \infty}f(x) = + \infty\)):
• At \(x = a\): \(f(a) = (a - a)(a - b) - 1 = - 1 < 0\).
• At \(x = b\): \(f(b) = (b - a)(b - b) - 1 = - 1 < 0\).
By the Intermediate Value Theorem:
1. Since \(\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow - \infty}f(x) = + \infty > 0\) and \(f(a) = - 1 < 0\), \(f(x) = 0\) has one real root in \(( - \infty,a)\).
2. Since \(f(b) = - 1 < 0\) and \(\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow + \infty}f(x) = + \infty > 0\), \(f(x) = 0\) has the second real root in \((b, + \infty)\).
Hence, option (D) is correct.
IIT200004111Q31:
For any complex number \(z_{k}\) with \(|z_{k}| = 1\), we have \(z_{k}{\overline{z}}_{k} = |z_{k}|^{2} = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{z_{k}} = {\overline{z}}_{k}\) for \(k = 1,2,3\).
Substituting \(\frac{1}{z_{k}} = {\overline{z}}_{k}\) into the given condition:
\[1 = \left| \frac{1}{z_{1}} + \frac{1}{z_{2}} + \frac{1}{z_{3}} \right| = |{\overline{z}}_{1} + {\overline{z}}_{2} + {\overline{z}}_{3}| = |\overline{z_{1} + z_{2} + z_{3}}|\]
Since the modulus of the conjugate of any complex number equals the modulus of the complex number itself (\(|\overline{w}| = |w|\)):
\[|z_{1} + z_{2} + z_{3}| = |\overline{z_{1} + z_{2} + z_{3}}| = 1\]
Hence, option (A) is correct.
IIT200004111Q32:
Let the roots of \(3x^{2} + px + 3 = 0\) be \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha^{2}\). By Vieta's formulas:
1. Product of roots: \(\alpha \cdot \alpha^{2} = \alpha^{3} = \frac{3}{3} = 1 \Rightarrow \alpha \in \{ 1,\omega,\omega^{2}\}\), where \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}\) is a non-real cube root of unity.
2. Sum of roots: \(\alpha + \alpha^{2} = - \frac{p}{3} \Rightarrow p = - 3(\alpha + \alpha^{2})\).
• If \(\alpha = 1\), then \(p = - 3(1 + 1) = - 6\), which contradicts the given condition \(p > 0\).
• If \(\alpha = \omega\) (or \(\omega^{2}\)), then using \(1 + \omega + \omega^{2} = 0 \Rightarrow \omega + \omega^{2} = - 1\):
\[p = - 3(\omega + \omega^{2}) = - 3( - 1) = 3 > 0\]
Hence, \(p = 3\), which corresponds to option (C).
IIT200004111Q33:
Rewriting the parabola \(y^{2} - kx + 8 = 0\) in standard vertex form (\(k \neq 0\)):
\[y^{2} = k\left( x - \frac{8}{k} \right)\]
Comparing this with \(Y^{2} = 4aX\) where \(Y = y\), \(X = x - \frac{8}{k}\), and \(4a = k \Rightarrow a = \frac{k}{4}\):
The equation of the directrix is \(X = - a\), which in terms of \(x\) is:
\[x - \frac{8}{k} = - \frac{k}{4} \Rightarrow x = \frac{8}{k} - \frac{k}{4}\]
Since the directrix is given as \(x = 1\):
\[\frac{8}{k} - \frac{k}{4} = 1 \Rightarrow 32 - k^{2} = 4k \Rightarrow k^{2} + 4k - 32 = 0\]
Factoring the quadratic:
\[(k + 8)(k - 4) = 0 \Rightarrow k = 4 \text{ or } k = - 8\]
Thus, one of the values of \(k\) is \(4\), which corresponds to option (C).
IIT200004111Q34:
Consider the auxiliary function \(h(x) = \log _{e}(1 + x) - x\) on \([ 0,1)\). Differentiating with respect to \(x\):
\[h'(x) = \frac{1}{1 + x} - 1 = - \frac{x}{1 + x}\]
For all \(x \in (0,1)\), we have \(x > 0\) and \(1 + x > 0\), so \(h'(x) < 0\). Therefore, \(h(x)\) is strictly decreasing on \([ 0,1)\).
Since \(h(0) = \log _{e}(1) - 0 = 0\), it follows that for all \(x \in (0,1)\):
\[h(x) < h(0) = 0 \Rightarrow \log _{e}(1 + x) < x\]
(Meanwhile, for \(x \in (0,1)\), \(e^{x} > 1 + x\), \(\sin x < x\), and \(\log _{e}x < 0 < x\), so A, C, D are all false.) Hence, option (B) is correct.
IIT200004111Q35:
Let \(t = \log _{e}x\). Then \(dt = \frac{1}{x} dx\).
Changing the limits of integration:
• When \(x = e^{- 1}\), \(t = \log _{e}(e^{- 1}) = - 1\).
• When \(x = e^{2}\), \(t = \log _{e}(e^{2}) = 2\).
Since \(x > 0\) on \([ e^{- 1},e^{2}]\), we have \(\left| \frac{\log _{e}x}{x} \right| dx = |t| dt\). Splitting the integral at \(t = 0\):
\[I = \int_{- 1}^{2}|t| dt = \int_{- 1}^{0}( - t) dt + \int_{0}^{2}t dt = \left[ - \frac{t^{2}}{2} \right]_{- 1}^{0} + \left[ \frac{t^{2}}{2} \right]_{0}^{2} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{4}{2} = \frac{5}{2}\]
Hence, option (B) is correct.
IIT200005070Q01a:
Let the four consecutive terms of the arithmetic progression with integer entries be:
\[a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d\]
where \(a \in {\mathbb{Z}}\) is the first of the four terms and \(d \in {\mathbb{Z}}\) is the common difference.
We need to consider the expression:
\[S = a(a + d)(a + 2d)(a + 3d) + d^{4}\]
Grouping the first and fourth factors together, and the second and third factors together:
\[\begin{gathered} a(a + 3d) = a^{2} + 3ad \\ (a + d)(a + 2d) = a^{2} + 3ad + 2d^{2} \end{gathered}\]
Let \(u = a^{2} + 3ad\). Since \(a,d \in {\mathbb{Z}}\), \(u\) is an integer. Substituting \(u\) into \(S\):
\[S = u(u + 2d^{2}) + d^{4} = u^{2} + 2ud^{2} + (d^{2})^{2} = (u + d^{2})^{2}\]
Substituting back \(u = a^{2} + 3ad\):
\[S = (a^{2} + 3ad + d^{2})^{2}\]
Since \(a\) and \(d\) are integers, \(N = a^{2} + 3ad + d^{2}\) is also an integer, and hence \(S = N^{2}\) is the square of an integer. Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q01b:
Part 1 (Hockey-Stick Identity):
Using Pascal's identity \(\dbinom{k + 1}{m + 1} - \dbinom{k}{m + 1} = \dbinom{k}{m}\) for \(k = m + 1,m + 2,\ldots,n\), and noting that \(\dbinom{m}{m} = 1 = \dbinom{m + 1}{m + 1}\), we rewrite the sum from right to left:
\[\text{LHS}_{1} = \dbinom{m}{m} + \dbinom{m + 1}{m} + \dbinom{m + 2}{m} + \cdots + \dbinom{n}{m}\]
Replacing \(\dbinom{m}{m}\) by \(\dbinom{m + 1}{m + 1}\) and repeatedly applying \(\dbinom{k}{m + 1} + \dbinom{k}{m} = \dbinom{k + 1}{m + 1}\):
\[\begin{gathered} \dbinom{m + 1}{m + 1} + \dbinom{m + 1}{m} = \dbinom{m + 2}{m + 1} \\ \dbinom{m + 2}{m + 1} + \dbinom{m + 2}{m} = \dbinom{m + 3}{m + 1} \end{gathered}\]
Continuing this telescoping cascade up to \(k = n\) yields:
\[\text{LHS}_{1} = \dbinom{n}{m + 1} + \dbinom{n}{m} = \dbinom{n + 1}{m + 1} = \text{RHS}_{1}\]
Part 2 (Weighted Binomial Sum):
Let \(S_{2} = \sum_{k = m}^{n}(n - k + 1)\dbinom{k}{m}\). Writing the terms in a triangular array gives:
\[S_{2} = \sum_{j = m}^{n}\left( \sum_{k = m}^{j}\dbinom{k}{m} \right)\]
By the Part 1 identity, the inner sum for each upper index \(j\) is \(\sum_{k = m}^{j}\dbinom{k}{m} = \dbinom{j + 1}{m + 1}\). Substituting this in:
\[S_{2} = \sum_{j = m}^{n}\dbinom{j + 1}{m + 1} = \dbinom{m + 1}{m + 1} + \dbinom{m + 2}{m + 1} + \cdots + \dbinom{n + 1}{m + 1}\]
Applying the Part 1 identity once again with \(m\) replaced by \(m + 1\) and \(n\) replaced by \(n + 1\):
\[S_{2} = \dbinom{(n + 1) + 1}{(m + 1) + 1} = \dbinom{n + 2}{m + 2}\]
Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q02a:
For the first quadratic equation \(ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\) (\(a \neq 0\)), by Vieta's formulas:
\[\alpha + \beta = - \frac{b}{a}, \alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}\]
Therefore, the square of the difference of its roots is:
\[(\alpha - \beta)^{2} = (\alpha + \beta)^{2} - 4\alpha\beta = \frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{4c}{a} = \frac{b^{2} - 4ac}{a^{2}} \cdots(1)\]
For the second quadratic equation \(Ax^{2} + Bx + C = 0\) (\(A \neq 0\)) with roots \(\alpha' = \alpha + \delta\) and \(\beta' = \beta + \delta\):
\[\alpha' + \beta' = - \frac{B}{A}, \alpha'\beta' = \frac{C}{A}\]
The square of the difference of its roots is:
\[(\alpha' - \beta')^{2} = (\alpha' + \beta')^{2} - 4\alpha'\beta' = \frac{B^{2} - 4AC}{A^{2}} \cdots(2)\]
However, translating both roots by the same constant \(\delta\) leaves their difference unchanged:
\[\alpha' - \beta' = (\alpha + \delta) - (\beta + \delta) = \alpha - \beta \Rightarrow (\alpha' - \beta')^{2} = (\alpha - \beta)^{2}\]
Equating \((1)\) and \((2)\) immediately yields:
\[\frac{b^{2} - 4ac}{a^{2}} = \frac{B^{2} - 4AC}{A^{2}}\]
Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q02b:
Part 1 (Inequality Proof):
Since \(n\) is a positive integer, \(\sqrt{4n + 1}\), \(\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1}\), and \(\sqrt{4n + 2}\) are all strictly positive. We compare their squares:
\[\left( \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1} \right)^{2} = 2n + 1 + 2\sqrt{n(n + 1)} = 2n + 1 + \sqrt{4n^{2} + 4n}\]
Observe that for every \(n \geq 1\):
\[(2n)^{2} = 4n^{2} < 4n^{2} + 4n < 4n^{2} + 4n + 1 = (2n + 1)^{2}\]
Taking positive square roots across this strict inequality gives:
\[2n < \sqrt{4n^{2} + 4n} < 2n + 1\]
Adding \(2n + 1\) throughout:
\[4n + 1 < 2n + 1 + \sqrt{4n^{2} + 4n} < 4n + 2 \Rightarrow 4n + 1 < \left( \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1} \right)^{2} < 4n + 2\]
Taking positive square roots across the inequality yields:
\[\sqrt{4n + 1} < \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1} < \sqrt{4n + 2}\]
Part 2 (Greatest Integer Equality):
Let \(k = \left[\sqrt{4n + 1}\right]\). Since \(\sqrt{4n + 1} < \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1} < \sqrt{4n + 2}\), the floor \(\left[\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1}\right]\) could exceed \(k\) only if there were an integer \(m = k + 1\) satisfying:
\[\sqrt{4n + 1} < m \leq \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1} < \sqrt{4n + 2}\]
Squaring this inequality would require:
\[4n + 1 < m^{2} < 4n + 2\]
However, \(4n + 1\) and \(4n + 2\) are consecutive integers, so no integer \(m^{2}\) can lie strictly between them (moreover, \(4n + 2 \equiv 2\text{ (mod }4\text{)}\) can never be a perfect square anyway, so \(\sqrt{4n + 2}\) is never an integer). Thus no integer lies in \((\sqrt{4n + 1},\sqrt{4n + 2}]\), which proves that:
\[\left[\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{n + 1}\right] = \left[\sqrt{4n + 1}\right]\]
Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q03a:
In any \(\triangle ABC\), we have \(A + B + C = \pi\), so:
\[\frac{A}{2} + \frac{B}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{C}{2}\]
Taking the cotangent of both sides and applying the cotangent addition formula \(\cot (x + y) = \frac{\cot x\cot y - 1}{\cot x + \cot y}\):
\[\begin{gathered} \cot \left( \frac{A}{2} + \frac{B}{2} \right) = \cot \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{C}{2} \right) = \tan \frac{C}{2} = \frac{1}{\cot \frac{C}{2}} \\ \frac{\cot \frac{A}{2}\cot \frac{B}{2} - 1}{\cot \frac{A}{2} + \cot \frac{B}{2}} = \frac{1}{\cot \frac{C}{2}} \end{gathered}\]
Cross-multiplying gives:
\[\cot \frac{A}{2}\cot \frac{B}{2}\cot \frac{C}{2} - \cot \frac{C}{2} = \cot \frac{A}{2} + \cot \frac{B}{2}\]
Rearranging terms yields:
\[\cot \frac{A}{2} + \cot \frac{B}{2} + \cot \frac{C}{2} = \cot \frac{A}{2}\cot \frac{B}{2}\cot \frac{C}{2}\]
Hence proved.

IIT200005070Q03b.t:
Consider the quadrilateral \(AFIE\). Since \(IF\bot AB\) and \(IE\bot AC\), the line \(AI\) bisects both \(\angle FAE = A\) and \(\angle FIE = \pi - A\).
Let \(I_{1}\) be the centre of the circle of radius \(r_{1}\) inscribed in quadrilateral \(AFIE\). By symmetry, \(I_{1}\) lies on the angle bisector segment \(AI\):
1. In the right triangle formed by dropping a perpendicular from \(I_{1}\) to \(AF\), since \(\angle I_{1}AF = \frac{A}{2}\):
\[AI_{1} = \frac{r_{1}}{\sin \frac{A}{2}}\]
2. In the right triangle formed by dropping a perpendicular from \(I_{1}\) to \(IF\), since \(\angle I_{1}IF = \frac{1}{2}\angle FIE = \frac{\pi - A}{2}\):
\[I_{1}I = \frac{r_{1}}{\sin \left( \frac{\pi - A}{2} \right)} = \frac{r_{1}}{\cos \frac{A}{2}}\]
3. Moreover, in right \(\triangle AFI\), we have \(AI = \frac{r}{\sin \frac{A}{2}}\), so the distance \(I_{1}I = AI - AI_{1}\) is also given by:
\[I_{1}I = \frac{r - r_{1}}{\sin \frac{A}{2}}\]
Equating the two expressions for \(I_{1}I\):
\[\frac{r - r_{1}}{\sin \frac{A}{2}} = \frac{r_{1}}{\cos \frac{A}{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{r_{1}}{r - r_{1}} = \frac{\cos \frac{A}{2}}{\sin \frac{A}{2}} = \cot \frac{A}{2}\]
Yes! \(\frac{\cos (A/2)}{\sin (A/2)} = \cot \frac{A}{2}\)!
Similarly, for quadrilaterals \(BDIF\) and \(CEID\):
\[\frac{r_{2}}{r - r_{2}} = \cot \frac{B}{2}, \frac{r_{3}}{r - r_{3}} = \cot \frac{C}{2}\]
Substituting these into the identity proved in Question 3(a), namely \(\cot \frac{A}{2} + \cot \frac{B}{2} + \cot \frac{C}{2} = \cot \frac{A}{2}\cot \frac{B}{2}\cot \frac{C}{2}\), we immediately obtain:
\[\frac{r_{1}}{r - r_{1}} + \frac{r_{2}}{r - r_{2}} + \frac{r_{3}}{r - r_{3}} = \frac{r_{1}r_{2}r_{3}}{(r - r_{1})(r - r_{2})(r - r_{3})}\]
Hence proved.

IIT200005070Q04.t:
Let \(P(x,y)\) be any point in the first quadrant (\(x \geq 0, y \geq 0\)).
The distance from \(P(x,y)\) to \(O(0,0)\) is:
\[d(P,O) = |x - 0| + |y - 0| = x + y\]
The distance from \(P(x,y)\) to \(A(3,2)\) is:
\[d(P,A) = |x - 3| + |y - 2|\]
Equating \(d(P,O) = d(P,A)\) gives:
\[x + y = |x - 3| + |y - 2|\]
We analyze the four sub-regions of the first quadrant determined by \(x \lessgtr 3\) and \(y \lessgtr 2\):
1. Case 1 (\(0 \leq x \leq 3\) and \(0 \leq y \leq 2\)):
Here \(|x - 3| = 3 - x\) and \(|y - 2| = 2 - y\). The equation becomes:
\[x + y = (3 - x) + (2 - y) \Rightarrow 2x + 2y = 5 \Rightarrow x + y = \frac{5}{2}\]
Intersecting the line \(x + y = \frac{5}{2}\) with the rectangle \([ 0,3] \times [ 0,2]\):
• At \(y = 2\), \(x = \frac{1}{2} \in [ 0,3]\), giving endpoint \(B\left( \frac{1}{2},2 \right)\).
• At \(y = 0\), \(x = \frac{5}{2} \in [ 0,3]\), giving endpoint \(C\left( \frac{5}{2},0 \right)\).
This gives the finite line segment \(BC\) joining \(B\left( \frac{1}{2},2 \right)\) and \(C\left( \frac{5}{2},0 \right)\) of Euclidean length \(\sqrt{(2)^{2} + ( - 2)^{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}\).
2. Case 2 (\(0 \leq x \leq 3\) and \(y \geq 2\)):
Here \(|x - 3| = 3 - x\) and \(|y - 2| = y - 2\). The equation becomes:
\[x + y = (3 - x) + (y - 2) \Rightarrow 2x = 1 \Rightarrow x = \frac{1}{2}\]
Since \(\frac{1}{2} \in [ 0,3]\), this gives the vertical infinite ray \(\left\{ \left( \frac{1}{2},y \right):y \geq 2 \right\}\) starting at \(B\left( \frac{1}{2},2 \right)\) and extending upward to \(+ \infty\).
3. Case 3 (\(x > 3\) and \(0 \leq y \leq 2\)):
Here \(|x - 3| = x - 3\) and \(|y - 2| = 2 - y\). The equation becomes:
\[x + y = (x - 3) + (2 - y) \Rightarrow 2y = - 1 \Rightarrow y = - \frac{1}{2}\]
Since \(y \geq 0\) in the first quadrant, there is no solution in this region.
4. Case 4 (\(x > 3\) and \(y > 2\)):
Here \(|x - 3| = x - 3\) and \(|y - 2| = y - 2\). The equation becomes:
\[x + y = x - 3 + y - 2 \Rightarrow 0 = - 5\]
which is impossible, giving no solution.
Combining all four cases, the locus in the first quadrant is the union of the finite line segment \(x + y = \frac{5}{2}\) (\(\frac{1}{2} \leq x \leq \frac{5}{2}\)) and the vertical infinite ray \(x = \frac{1}{2}\) (\(y \geq 2\)). Hence proved.

IIT200005070Q05a:
Apply the row operation \(R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2} + R_{3}\). Using the sum-to-product identities on the three columns of \(R_{2} + R_{3}\):
1. First column:
\[\sin \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) + \sin \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) = 2\sin \theta\cos \frac{2\pi}{3} = 2\sin \theta\left( - \frac{1}{2} \right) = - \sin \theta\]
2. Second column:
\[\cos \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) + \cos \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) = 2\cos \theta\cos \frac{2\pi}{3} = 2\cos \theta\left( - \frac{1}{2} \right) = - \cos \theta\]
3. Third column:
\[\sin \left( 2\theta + \frac{4\pi}{3} \right) + \sin \left( 2\theta - \frac{4\pi}{3} \right) = 2\sin 2\theta\cos \frac{4\pi}{3} = 2\sin 2\theta\left( - \frac{1}{2} \right) = - \sin 2\theta\]
Now performing \(R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2} + R_{3} + R_{1}\), every entry in the second row becomes \(0\):
\[\Delta = \left| \begin{matrix} \sin \theta & \cos \theta & \sin 2\theta \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \sin \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) & \cos \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) & \sin \left( 2\theta - \frac{4\pi}{3} \right) \end{matrix} \right| = 0\]
Since an entire row of the determinant vanishes for all \(\theta \in {\mathbb{R}}\), \(\Delta = 0\) identically. Hence proved.

IIT200005070Q05b.t:
The circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\) is the auxiliary circle of the ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1\) (\(a > b\)).
Since \(\triangle ABC\) is an equilateral triangle inscribed in \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\), its vertices \(A,B,C\) have angular coordinates differing by \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\):
\[A = (a\cos \theta, a\sin \theta), B = \left( a\cos \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right), a\sin \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \right), C = \left( a\cos \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right), a\sin \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \right)\]
Since \(P,Q,R\) are the points on the ellipse with the same \(x\)-coordinates and lying on the same side of the major axis (\(x\)-axis) as \(A,B,C\) respectively, their eccentric angles on the ellipse are \(\theta\), \(\theta + \frac{2\pi}{3}\), and \(\theta - \frac{2\pi}{3}\):
\[P = (a\cos \theta, b\sin \theta), Q = \left( a\cos \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right), b\sin \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \right), R = \left( a\cos \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right), b\sin \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \right)\]
The equation of the normal to the ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1\) at a point with eccentric angle \(\phi\) is:
\[\frac{ax}{\cos \phi} - \frac{by}{\sin \phi} = a^{2} - b^{2} \Leftrightarrow (ax)\sin \phi - (by)\cos \phi - \frac{a^{2} - b^{2}}{2}\sin 2\phi = 0\]
Writing this equation for \(\phi_{1} = \theta\), \(\phi_{2} = \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3}\), and \(\phi_{3} = \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3}\), the determinant of coefficients of the three normal lines is:
\[D = \left| \begin{matrix} ax\sin \theta & - by\cos \theta & - \frac{a^{2} - b^{2}}{2}\sin 2\theta \\ ax\sin \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) & - by\cos \left( \theta + \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) & - \frac{a^{2} - b^{2}}{2}\sin \left( 2\theta + \frac{4\pi}{3} \right) \\ ax\sin \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) & - by\cos \left( \theta - \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) & - \frac{a^{2} - b^{2}}{2}\sin \left( 2\theta - \frac{4\pi}{3} \right) \end{matrix} \right|\]
Factoring out the constants from the three columns and using the result of Question 5(a) (\(\Delta = 0\)):
\[L_{P} + L_{Q} + L_{R} = 0\]
where \(L_{P} = 0\), \(L_{Q} = 0\), and \(L_{R} = 0\) are the equations of the three normals written in the form \((ax)\sin \phi_{i} - (by)\cos \phi_{i} - \frac{a^{2} - b^{2}}{2}\sin 2\phi_{i} = 0\). Since the three non-parallel normal lines satisfy the linear dependence \(1 \cdot L_{P} + 1 \cdot L_{Q} + 1 \cdot L_{R} \equiv 0\), any point of intersection of \(L_{P} = 0\) and \(L_{Q} = 0\) automatically lies on \(L_{R} = 0\). Thus, the normals at \(P,Q,R\) are concurrent. Hence proved.

IIT200005070Q06.t:
Part 1 (Reflection Property):
Let \(P(x_{1},y_{1})\) lie on \(C_{1}\), so \(x_{1}^{2} = y_{1} - 1\). Its reflection across the line \(y = x\) is \(P_{1}(y_{1},x_{1})\). Substituting the coordinates \((X,Y) = (y_{1},x_{1})\) of \(P_{1}\) into the equation of \(C_{2}\) (\(Y^{2} = X - 1\)):
\[Y^{2} - (X - 1) = x_{1}^{2} - (y_{1} - 1) = 0\]
Thus \(P_{1}\) lies on \(C_{2}\). Similarly, if \(Q(x_{2},y_{2})\) lies on \(C_{2}\), then \(y_{2}^{2} = x_{2} - 1\), so its reflection \(Q_{1}(y_{2},x_{2})\) across \(y = x\) satisfies \(X^{2} = y_{2}^{2} = x_{2} - 1 = Y - 1\), proving \(Q_{1}\) lies on \(C_{1}\).
Part 2 (Inequality \(PQ \geq \min \{ PP_{1},QQ_{1}\}\)):
For any point \(P(x_{1},y_{1}) \in C_{1}\), we have \(y_{1} - x_{1} = x_{1}^{2} + 1 - x_{1} = \left( x_{1} - \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4} > 0\), so \(C_{1}\) lies strictly in the upper half-plane \(y > x\).
Similarly, for any \(Q(x_{2},y_{2}) \in C_{2}\), \(x_{2} - y_{2} = \left( y_{2} - \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4} > 0\), so \(C_{2}\) lies strictly in the lower half-plane \(y < x\).
Let \(L\) be the line \(y = x\), and let \(d(P,L) = \frac{1}{2}PP_{1}\) and \(d(Q,L) = \frac{1}{2}QQ_{1}\) denote the perpendicular distances of \(P\) and \(Q\) from \(L\). Since \(P\) and \(Q\) lie on opposite sides of \(L\), the segment \(PQ\) intersects \(L\) at some point \(M \in L\). By the triangle inequality and perpendicular distance minimality:
\[PQ = PM + MQ \geq d(P,L) + d(Q,L) = \frac{1}{2}PP_{1} + \frac{1}{2}QQ_{1} \geq \min \{ PP_{1},QQ_{1}\}\]
Part 3 (Closest Points \(P_{0}\) and \(Q_{0}\)):
From Part 2, for any \(P(x_{1},y_{1}) \in C_{1}\):
\[PP_{1} = \sqrt{(x_{1} - y_{1})^{2} + (y_{1} - x_{1})^{2}} = \sqrt{2}(y_{1} - x_{1}) = \sqrt{2}\left[ \left( x_{1} - \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4} \right] \geq \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\]
with equality if and only if \(x_{1} = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(y_{1} = \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{2} + 1 = \frac{5}{4}\).
By symmetry, \(QQ_{1} \geq \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\) with equality at \(Q_{0} = \left( \frac{5}{4},\frac{1}{2} \right)\), which is the reflection of \(P_{0} = \left( \frac{1}{2},\frac{5}{4} \right)\) across \(y = x\).
Therefore, for all \(P \in C_{1}\) and \(Q \in C_{2}\):
\[PQ \geq \min \{ PP_{1},QQ_{1}\} \geq \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4} = P_{0}Q_{0}\]
Thus the unique points minimizing the distance are:
\[P_{0} = \left( \frac{1}{2},\frac{5}{4} \right) \in C_{1}, Q_{0} = \left( \frac{5}{4},\frac{1}{2} \right) \in C_{2}\]

IIT200005070Q07a:
First, evaluate the given inequality at \(x = 1\):
\[|P(1)| \leq |e^{1 - 1} - 1| = |e^{0} - 1| = 0 \Rightarrow P(1) = 0\]
Next, notice that the expression we need to bound is the derivative of \(P(x)\) at \(x = 1\):
\[P'(x) = a_{1} + 2a_{2}x + 3a_{3}x^{2} + \cdots + na_{n}x^{n - 1} \Rightarrow P'(1) = a_{1} + 2a_{2} + \cdots + na_{n}\]
For any \(x > 0\) with \(x \neq 1\), dividing both sides of \(|P(x)| \leq |e^{x - 1} - 1|\) by \(|x - 1| > 0\) and using \(P(1) = 0\):
\[\left| \frac{P(x) - P(1)}{x - 1} \right| \leq \left| \frac{e^{x - 1} - 1}{x - 1} \right|\]
Taking the limit as \(x \rightarrow 1\) on both sides (since \(P(x)\) is differentiable at \(x = 1\) and the absolute value function is continuous):
\[|P'(1)| = \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 1}\left| \frac{P(x) - P(1)}{x - 1} \right| \leq \lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 1}\left| \frac{e^{x - 1} - 1}{x - 1} \right| = |1| = 1\]
Substituting \(P'(1) = a_{1} + 2a_{2} + \cdots + na_{n}\) gives:
\[|a_{1} + 2a_{2} + \cdots + na_{n}| \leq 1\]
Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q07b:
In the integral defining \(f\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = \int_{1}^{1/x}\frac{\ln t}{1 + t} dt\), perform the substitution \(t = \frac{1}{u}\), so that \(dt = - \frac{1}{u^{2}} du\):
• When \(t = 1\), \(u = 1\).
• When \(t = \frac{1}{x}\), \(u = x\).
Therefore:
\[f\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = \int_{1}^{x}\frac{\ln (1/u)}{1 + \frac{1}{u}}\left( - \frac{1}{u^{2}} du \right) = \int_{1}^{x}\frac{- \ln u}{\frac{u + 1}{u}}\left( - \frac{1}{u^{2}} du \right) = \int_{1}^{x}\frac{\ln u}{u(1 + u)} du\]
Changing the dummy variable \(u\) back to \(t\) and adding \(f(x)\) and \(f\left( \frac{1}{x} \right)\):
\[f(x) + f\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = \int_{1}^{x}\left( \frac{\ln t}{1 + t} + \frac{\ln t}{t(1 + t)} \right) dt = \int_{1}^{x}\frac{(t + 1)\ln t}{t(1 + t)} dt = \int_{1}^{x}\frac{\ln t}{t} dt\]
Using the substitution \(w = \ln t\) (\(dw = \frac{1}{t} dt\)):
\[f(x) + f\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = \left[ \frac{(\ln t)^{2}}{2} \right]_{1}^{x} = \frac{1}{2}(\ln x)^{2}\]
Setting \(x = e\) (where \(\ln e = 1\)) gives:
\[f(e) + f\left( \frac{1}{e} \right) = \frac{1}{2}(\ln e)^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\]
Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q08:
Let \(P_{0}\) be the initial population at \(t = 0\), and let \(c\) be the constant annual food requirement per person.
1. Population & Total Food Requirement after \(n\) years:
Since population \(P(t)\) grows continuously at \(3\%\) per year:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.03P \Rightarrow P(t) = P_{0}e^{0.03t}\]
After \(n\) years, the total annual food requirement of the country is:
\[R_{n} = c \cdot P(n) = cP_{0}e^{0.03n}\]
2. Initial & \(n\)-th Year Food Production:
At \(t = 0\), the country has a \(10\%\) food deficit, meaning initial food production \(F_{0}\) is \(90\%\) of the initial food requirement \(R_{0} = cP_{0}\):
\[F_{0} = 0.90 cP_{0} = \frac{9}{10}cP_{0}\]
Since annual food production increases by \(4\%\) each year over the previous year, after \(n\) years:
\[F_{n} = F_{0}(1 + 0.04)^{n} = \frac{9}{10}cP_{0}(1.04)^{n}\]
3. Condition for Self-Sufficiency:
The country becomes self-sufficient in food when annual production meets or exceeds annual requirement (\(F_{n} \geq R_{n}\)):
\[\frac{9}{10}cP_{0}(1.04)^{n} \geq cP_{0}e^{0.03n} \Rightarrow \frac{(1.04)^{n}}{e^{0.03n}} \geq \frac{10}{9}\]
Taking natural logarithms (\(\ln\)) on both sides:
\[n\ln (1.04) - 0.03n \geq \ln 10 - \ln 9 \Rightarrow n\left( \ln (1.04) - 0.03 \right) \geq \ln 10 - \ln 9\]
Since \(\ln (1.04) \approx 0.03922 > 0.03\), the coefficient \(\ln (1.04) - 0.03 > 0\). Dividing by it gives:
\[n \geq \frac{\ln 10 - \ln 9}{\ln (1.04) - 0.03}\]
Thus, the country becomes self-sufficient after \(n\) years, where \(n\) is the smallest integer greater than or equal to \(\frac{\ln 10 - \ln 9}{\ln (1.04) - 0.03}\). Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q09a:
Let \(H\) denote Head (probability \(p\)) and \(T\) denote Tail (probability \(q = 1 - p\)). Let \(E_{n}\) be the event that no two (or more) consecutive heads occur in \(n\) independent tosses, so \(p_{n} = P(E_{n})\).
1. For \(n = 1\): A single toss (\(H\) or \(T\)) cannot contain two consecutive heads, so \(p_{1} = P(E_{1}) = 1\).
2. For \(n = 2\): The only outcome with two consecutive heads in \(2\) tosses is \(HH\), which has probability \(p^{2}\). Therefore:
\[p_{2} = 1 - P(HH) = 1 - p^{2}\]
3. For \(n \geq 3\): Partition the event \(E_{n}\) into two mutually exclusive cases based on the outcome of the first toss:
• Case 1 (First toss is \(T\), probability \(1 - p\)): The remaining \(n - 1\) tosses can be any sequence with no two consecutive heads, which occurs with conditional probability \(p_{n - 1}\). Contribution: \((1 - p)p_{n - 1}\).
• **Case 2 (First toss is \(H\), probability \(p\)):* To avoid two consecutive heads at the start, the second toss must* be \(T\) (probability \(1 - p\)), and the remaining \(n - 2\) tosses must contain no two consecutive heads (probability \(p_{n - 2}\)). Contribution: \(p(1 - p)p_{n - 2}\).
By the Law of Total Probability, adding the two mutually exclusive cases yields:
\[p_{n} = (1 - p)p_{n - 1} + p(1 - p)p_{n - 2} \text{forall}n \geq 3\]
Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q09b:
Since \(\alpha,\beta\) are the roots of \(x^{2} - (1 - p)x - p(1 - p) = 0\), they satisfy Vieta's relations:
\[\alpha + \beta = 1 - p, \alpha\beta = - p(1 - p)\]
and each root satisfies the characteristic equation:
\[\alpha^{2} = (1 - p)\alpha + p(1 - p), \beta^{2} = (1 - p)\beta + p(1 - p)\]
Base Cases (\(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\)):
Notice that the expressions for \(A\) and \(B\) can be written as:
\[A\alpha = \frac{p^{2} + \beta - 1}{\beta - \alpha}, B\beta = \frac{p^{2} + \alpha - 1}{\alpha - \beta}\]
• For \(n = 1\):
\[A\alpha + B\beta = \frac{(p^{2} + \beta - 1) - (p^{2} + \alpha - 1)}{\beta - \alpha} = \frac{\beta - \alpha}{\beta - \alpha} = 1 = p_{1}\]
• For \(n = 2\):
\[A\alpha^{2} + B\beta^{2} = \frac{\alpha(p^{2} + \beta - 1) - \beta(p^{2} + \alpha - 1)}{\beta - \alpha} = \frac{(\alpha - \beta)(p^{2} - 1)}{\beta - \alpha} = 1 - p^{2} = p_{2}\]
Thus the formula holds for \(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\).
Inductive Step:
Assume that for some \(k \geq 3\), the formula \(p_{m} = A\alpha^{m} + B\beta^{m}\) holds for \(m = k - 2\) and \(m = k - 1\). Using the recurrence relation from 9(a):
\[\begin{gathered} p_{k} = (1 - p)p_{k - 1} + p(1 - p)p_{k - 2} \\ p_{k} = (1 - p)\left( A\alpha^{k - 1} + B\beta^{k - 1} \right) + p(1 - p)\left( A\alpha^{k - 2} + B\beta^{k - 2} \right) \end{gathered}\]
Grouping the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) terms:
\[p_{k} = A\alpha^{k - 2}\left[ (1 - p)\alpha + p(1 - p) \right] + B\beta^{k - 2}\left[ (1 - p)\beta + p(1 - p) \right]\]
Using \(\alpha^{2} = (1 - p)\alpha + p(1 - p)\) and \(\beta^{2} = (1 - p)\beta + p(1 - p)\):
\[p_{k} = A\alpha^{k - 2} \cdot \alpha^{2} + B\beta^{k - 2} \cdot \beta^{2} = A\alpha^{k} + B\beta^{k}\]
By the Principle of Strong Mathematical Induction, \(p_{n} = A\alpha^{n} + B\beta^{n}\) holds for all \(n \geq 1\). Hence proved.
IIT200005070Q10:
Choose the point of concurrency \(O\) of the perpendiculars from \(A,B,C\) to the sides \(QR,RP,PQ\) as the origin of position vectors. Let the position vectors of \(A,B,C\) and \(P,Q,R\) with respect to \(O\) be \(\overset{\rightarrow}{a},\overset{\rightarrow}{b},\overset{\rightarrow}{c}\) and \(\overset{\rightarrow}{p},\overset{\rightarrow}{q},\overset{\rightarrow}{r}\) respectively.
1. Since \(OA\bot QR\), \(OB\bot RP\), and \(OC\bot PQ\), their dot products vanish:
\[\overset{\rightarrow}{a} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{r} - \overset{\rightarrow}{q}\right) = 0, \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{p} - \overset{\rightarrow}{r}\right) = 0, \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{q} - \overset{\rightarrow}{p}\right) = 0\]
2. Adding these three equations and regrouping the dot products by \(\overset{\rightarrow}{p},\overset{\rightarrow}{q},\overset{\rightarrow}{r}\):
\[\begin{gathered} \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{r} - \overset{\rightarrow}{a} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{q} + \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{p} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{r} + \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{q} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c} \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{p} = 0 \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{p} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{b} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right) + \overset{\rightarrow}{q} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{c} - \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\right) + \overset{\rightarrow}{r} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\right) = 0 \cdots(*) \end{gathered}\]
Now let \(O'\) (with position vector \(\overset{\rightarrow}{x}\)) be the point of intersection of the perpendiculars from \(P\) to \(BC\) and from \(Q\) to \(CA\):
• Since \(O'P\bot BC\): \(\left(\overset{\rightarrow}{p} - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}\right) \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{c} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\right) = 0 \Rightarrow \overset{\rightarrow}{p} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{b} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right) = \overset{\rightarrow}{x} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{b} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right)\).
• Since \(O'Q\bot CA\): \(\left(\overset{\rightarrow}{q} - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}\right) \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right) = 0 \Rightarrow \overset{\rightarrow}{q} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{c} - \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\right) = \overset{\rightarrow}{x} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{c} - \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\right)\).
Substituting these two relations into identity \((*)\):
\[\begin{gathered} \overset{\rightarrow}{x} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{b} - \overset{\rightarrow}{c}\right) + \overset{\rightarrow}{x} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{c} - \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\right) + \overset{\rightarrow}{r} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\right) = 0 \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{x} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{b} - \overset{\rightarrow}{a}\right) + \overset{\rightarrow}{r} \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\right) = 0 \Rightarrow \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{r} - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}\right) \cdot \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\right) = 0 \end{gathered}\]
This states that the vector \(\overset{\rightarrow}{O'R} = \overset{\rightarrow}{r} - \overset{\rightarrow}{x}\) is perpendicular to \(\overset{\rightarrow}{BA} = \overset{\rightarrow}{a} - \overset{\rightarrow}{b}\), meaning the line \(O'R\) is perpendicular to side \(AB\). Therefore, the perpendicular from \(R\) to \(AB\) also passes through \(O'\), proving that the perpendiculars from \(P,Q,R\) to \(BC,CA,AB\) are concurrent. Hence proved.

IIT200104111Q01.t:
To find where \(f(x) = \max \left\{ x,x^{3} \right\}\) fails to be differentiable, we first solve \(x^{3} = x\), which gives \(x\left( x^{2} - 1 \right) = 0 \Rightarrow x = - 1,0,1\).
Comparing \(x\) and \(x^{3}\) on the resulting intervals yields the piecewise definition:
\(f(x) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} x, & x < - 1 \\ x^{3}, & - 1 \leq x < 0 \\ x, & 0 \leq x < 1 \\ x^{3}, & x \geq 1 \end{matrix} \right.\)
Since \(x\) and \(x^{3}\) are polynomials, \(f(x)\) is continuous everywhere on \(\mathbb{R}\) and differentiable on \(\mathbb{R} \smallsetminus \left\{ - 1,0,1 \right\}\), with derivative:
\(f^{\prime}(x) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} 1, & x < - 1 \\ 3x^{2}, & - 1 < x < 0 \\ 1, & 0 < x < 1 \\ 3x^{2}, & x > 1 \end{matrix} \right.\)
Checking the left-hand and right-hand derivatives at each transition point:
• At \(x = - 1\): \(f^{\prime}\left( - 1^{-} \right) = 1\) and \(f^{\prime}\left( - 1^{+} \right) = 3( - 1)^{2} = 3\). Since \(1 \neq 3\), \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = - 1\).
• At \(x = 0\): \(f^{\prime}\left( 0^{-} \right) = 3(0)^{2} = 0\) and \(f^{\prime}\left( 0^{+} \right) = 1\). Since \(0 \neq 1\), \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = 0\).
• At \(x = 1\): \(f^{\prime}\left( 1^{-} \right) = 1\) and \(f^{\prime}\left( 1^{+} \right) = 3(1)^{2} = 3\). Since \(1 \neq 3\), \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = 1\).
Therefore, the set of all points where \(f(x)\) is not differentiable is \(\left\{ - 1,0,1 \right\}\).
